title: Relational Anchors for Quantum Subsystem Identification: Minimal Separation and Robust Rigidity
abstract: Operational data can be complete inside a chosen subsystem frame while leaving the frame itself non-unique. A previous finite certification construction exhibits this phenomenon explicitly: an unpartitioned three-qubit Pauli presentation supports three inequivalent finest full tensor frames even though its generated observable algebra is all of M_8(\mathbb C). We ask what additional information can select one frame without treating that information as merely another unlabelled control direction. We introduce relational anchors: gauge-equivariant constraints on a finite refinement poset of direction-generated frames. A general finite-poset theorem characterizes exact anchor collapse and turns target certification into a hitting-set problem, while global frame identification becomes a test-cover problem. In the three-qubit presentation we enumerate the complete nontrivial full witness poset, prove that one two-direction locality anchor separates all three finest frames, and determine exactly twelve single anchors of this type that pass the full-poset test. For robustness, exact support is replaced by conditional-expectation signatures, yielding a sharp \gamma/2 separation criterion. We prove a zero-radius result for the exact witness poset under unrestricted raw perturbations and derive a sharp projective Pauli decoding radius. Six Hamiltonian-derivation squares reconstruct the projective Pauli geometry. A residual synchronization analysis separates ordinary graph cycles from gauge-invariant parity constraints, and four atomic Jordan–Lie anchors are necessary and sufficient, within the declared anchor class, to reduce the remaining scale and sign freedom to Clifford gauge. An explicit relative-defect rigidity modulus and a protocol-conditioned end-to-end error certificate are obtained. The result does not claim that probabilities alone determine a physical tensor-product structure. Rather, unpartitioned process data together with a finite relational anchor package robustly identify a subsystem frame up to the declared gauge.

title: Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Optimization and Differential Equations
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. However, its efficacy is significantly hampered when the underlying systems are described by differential equations. Traditional SR methods often fail to identify accurate equations due to the inherent complexity and non-linearity of these systems. This work proposes a novel approach that combines symbolic regression with Bayesian optimization and differential equation solvers to overcome this limitation. The core idea is to leverage Bayesian optimization to intelligently explore the space of possible mathematical expressions while incorporating differential equation solvers to validate and refine these expressions. This integrated framework allows for the discovery of accurate mathematical models for systems governed by differential equations, addressing a critical gap in the current SR landscape. We outline the methodology, provide a theoretical justification, and discuss potential applications.

title: Adaptive Kernel Methods with Dynamic Feature Selection based on Information Gain
abstract: Kernel methods have proven to be powerful tools in machine learning, particularly for tackling non-linear classification problems. However, their success is often contingent upon the careful selection of kernel functions and their associated parameters, a process that can be computationally expensive and prone to suboptimal results. This paper proposes a novel adaptive kernel learning algorithm that dynamically selects and adapts kernel functions and parameters based on information gain. The core idea is to identify features that contribute most to the classification task, thereby optimizing the kernel's effectiveness in representing the underlying data distribution. The algorithm iteratively refines the kernel function and its parameters by maximizing the information gain associated with each feature, leading to improved classification accuracy and reduced computational complexity. The key innovations lie in the dynamic feature selection process and the adaptive nature of the kernel parameters, offering a more robust and efficient approach to kernel learning compared to traditional methods. This work demonstrates the potential of combining kernel learning with adaptive feature selection for achieving superior performance in various classification scenarios.

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Dynamic Optimization of Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic reasoning by integrating Bayesian Networks (BNs) with Logic Programming. Traditional approaches to probabilistic logic programming often struggle with efficiently managing and optimizing the complex relationships between variables, leading to performance bottlenecks and potentially inaccurate inferences. Our core claim is that dynamic optimization of BNs, leveraging the structured reasoning capabilities of logic programming, significantly improves both inference efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism involves utilizing Bayesian Networks for probabilistic inference and Logic Programming for modeling and optimizing variable relationships. We introduce a framework where logical constraints derived from a knowledge base are translated into a BN structure, and then dynamically adjusted during inference to minimize computational cost and maximize accuracy. The key innovation lies in the iterative refinement of the BN graph and associated probabilities, guided by logical rules and constraints, thereby addressing a critical gap in existing probabilistic logic programming methodologies. This approach offers a pathway towards more scalable and robust probabilistic reasoning systems, particularly in domains with evolving knowledge and complex intervariable dependencies.

title: Dynamic Topological Semantic Networks (DTSN)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topological Semantic Networks (DTSN), a novel approach to dynamic system understanding. DTSN leverages continuous, context-aware topological learning to achieve a dynamic semantic understanding of complex system states, surpassing the limitations of static data models and traditional knowledge representation. The core mechanism involves a Graph Neural Network (GNN) engine that learns both static and dynamic attributes of nodes and edges, interpreting node interactions (communication, data sharing, dependencies) as topological changes. These changes are reflected in real-time updates of semantic weights within the GNN. Furthermore, DTSN incorporates a "semantic drift" detection mechanism to identify underlying semantic shifts within topological changes, triggering knowledge updates and reasoning. The novelty of DTSN lies in its ability to perform adaptive semantic modeling through GNN-based graph learning and its proactive handling of semantic drift, a relatively unexplored area in computer science research. The system aims to provide a robust and adaptable framework for modeling and reasoning about complex, evolving systems where traditional static approaches fall short. ---

title: Dynamically Adaptive Neural Architecture Search via Evolutionary Strategies with Bayesian Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Neural Architecture Search (NAS) that leverages the strengths of both evolutionary strategies and Bayesian optimization. Traditional NAS methods often suffer from high computational costs due to exhaustive or near-exhaustive searches of the architecture space. Our proposed algorithm, Dynamically Adaptive Neural Architecture Search (DANA), utilizes evolutionary strategies for broad exploration combined with Bayesian optimization to dynamically adjust the search focus based on performance feedback. This adaptive mechanism concentrates computational effort on promising architectural regions, significantly reducing the overall search time and improving the efficiency of architecture discovery. We formulate the NAS problem as an optimization problem, aiming to find the architecture that maximizes a predefined performance metric. The core of our approach lies in the iterative refinement process, where evolutionary strategies generate candidate architectures, Bayesian optimization evaluates them, and the results inform the next generation of evolutionary strategies. The efficacy of DANA is demonstrated through simulations, showcasing its ability to achieve competitive or superior performance compared to existing NAS methods with substantially reduced computational resources. The algorithm's dynamic adaptation provides a critical advantage in navigating complex architectural spaces, leading to faster convergence and more effective architecture discovery.

title: Silicon microring resonator for photonic neural networks
abstract: Photonic neural networks (PNNs) have emerged as a promising hardware platform for artificial intelligence by exploiting the high bandwidth, inherent parallelism, and low latency of optical computing. Among integrated photonic devices, silicon microring resonators, with their compact footprint and compatibility with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) fabrication, have been widely investigated for implementing modulation and weighting. However, previous practical PNN systems for a specific task, such as image classification, have separated sensing and computing units, which limits the system performance. Furthermore, a practical PNN requires more than modulation and weighting. A nonlinear activation function is a necessary module for implementing multilayer neural networks, while reliable chip packaging is required to achieve a standalone integrated system. title: QC-CCG: Quantum-Classical Algorithm for Two-stage Adaptive Robust Optimization
abstract: Quantum optimization provides a promising approach for solving large-scale combinatorial problems through quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulations. However, integrating QUBO-based solvers into structured optimization frameworks while preserving solution guarantees remains a fundamental challenge. This paper develops a hybrid quantum-classical column-and-constraint generation (QCCG) framework for solving two-stage adaptive robust optimization problems with binary first-stage decisions and linear recourse under polyhedral uncertainty. The proposed approach reformulates the restricted master problem as a QUBO and solves it approximately using a quantum optimizer, while retaining a classical adversarial subproblem to compute worst-case recourse and certify solution quality. We construct a constraint-preserving QUBO encoding for inequality-constrained master problems using slack variables and penalty terms, enabling general mixed-integer structures to be mapped to quantum-compatible representations. To address inexactness arising from discretization, penalty modeling, and quantum optimization, we introduce a bound-adjustment mechanism that yields valid lower and upper bounds and provides a certified stopping criterion. We show that the proposed framework generalizes classical column-and-constraint generation and retains its convergence properties when the master problem is solved exactly. Numerical experiments on two-stage robust location-transportation problems demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach achieves solution quality comparable to classical methods while reducing the computational burden associated with solving mixed-integer master problems, highlighting the potential of hybrid quantum-classical optimization for scalable decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Spatial-Semantic Reasoning using Large Language Models for Efficient UAV Search Operations
abstract: We present a real-time semantic navigation framework for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) focused on improving time efficiency in the Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) task. Central to our approach is a Large Language Model (LLM) that interprets user-provided natural language instructions and performs semantic reasoning over detected objects and spatial context to prioritize high-probability search regions. The system combines real-time object detection, 3D spatial mapping, and polynomial spline interpolation for smooth and feasible UAV trajectory planning. Unlike prior methods that rely on offline reasoning or simulator-constrained action spaces, our framework can operate in real time, continuously updating semantic relevance based on new observations. Experiments in both simulated and real-world settings demonstrate reductions in mission duration while maintaining high search accuracy, underscoring the effectiveness of LLM-guided reasoning for time- efficient UAV-based ObjectNav.

title: Should I Use This Synthetic Dataset for Training? How to Test with Minimal Real Data
abstract: Digital twins (DTs) and learned world models are increasingly used to generate synthetic data that augment the scarce real datasets available for training artificial intelligence (AI) models in engineering systems. Owing to the inevitable simulation-to-reality (sim-to-real) gap, however, augmentation may fail to improve the performance of the trained model on the real data distribution. This paper addresses the resulting decision problem: Given a real dataset, a candidate synthetic dataset, and a fixed learning algorithm, decide whether training on the augmented dataset improves the true, population-level performance, while consuming as few real test data points as possible. Two formulations are considered: a direct test on the mean loss difference between the two trained models, and a symmetry-based test on the paired loss difference, which trades a stronger null assumption for faster evidence accumulation. For the latter, we introduce the {adaptive e-process sign-flip test} (aeSFT), a doubly adaptive procedure that adapts both the number of Monte Carlo sign-flip rounds, and hence the computational cost, and the amount of real test data consumed. aeSFT yields anytime-valid Type-I error control, with no need to pre-specify the test-set size. Experiments on a synthetic-data classification task, a DT-aided wireless packet-scheduling task, and a radio-map prediction task show that aeSFT identifies useful synthetic data using substantially fewer real test samples than mean-based sequential testing, matches the power of fixed-sample sign-flip testing and the paired $t$-test, while keeping the false-positive rate below the target level.

title: Secure Artificial Intelligence for Asset Performance in Critical Infrastructure: A Critical Narrative Review of Safety, Operational Excellence and Continuous Quality Improvement
abstract: Critical infrastructure operators increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) to detect degradation, predict failures, optimise maintenance, identify cyber anomalies and support operational decisions. These capabilities create a plausible route to higher availability, reliability and quality, yet they also couple asset-performance decisions to data integrity, model uncertainty, software supply chains, human oversight and operational technology security. This critical narrative review examines how secure AI can contribute to asset performance without weakening safety or resilience. Literature spanning predictive maintenance and prognostics, industrial AI, digital twins, industrial cyber-physical security, adversarial machine learning, explainability, uncertainty, machine-learning operations and human factors was critically synthesised. The evidence is strongest for AI as a decision-support layer for condition monitoring, fault diagnosis and targeted maintenance where data provenance is controlled, failure modes are sufficiently represented and recommendations remain bounded by engineering constraints. Evidence for fully autonomous optimisation in high-consequence infrastructure is less mature because benchmark accuracy does not directly establish operational utility, transferability or safe behaviour under distribution shift and hostile manipulation. Digital twins can improve contextual diagnosis and testing, but their value depends on fidelity, synchronisation, governance and protection of the data-model-actuation pathway. Cybersecurity and safety therefore cannot be treated as independent assurance domains: poisoned training data, adversarial inputs, compromised updates or unavailable models can become physical reliability and quality risks. Explainability alone is also insufficient for assurance; uncertainty calibration, abstention, independent validation, auditability and meaningful human authority are required. The synthesis proposes a secure asset-performance loop in which AI recommendations are evaluated against safety, security, service and quality constraints, with outcomes fed back into monitored model and process improvement. The central implication is that asset performance should be maximised as a constrained socio-technical objective rather than as an unconstrained prediction or utilisation metric.

title: Formula-State Transformer: Residual-Preserving Relational Workspaces for Stable Evidence Fusion
abstract: This record contains preprint v1.0 of “Formula-State Transformer: Residual-Preserving Relational Workspaces for Stable Evidence Fusion,” together with the complete architecture code, controlled-experiment outputs, causal-intervention results, a 10-million-character language-modeling dataset and evaluation, publication figures, software-environment information, reproducibility documentation, and a file-level SHA-256 manifest. The Formula-State Transformer v3 (FST v3) augments a standard causal Transformer with an iterative, query-conditioned relational workspace. The ordinary Transformer residual stream is preserved in full. The workspace accumulates interactions among evidence paths, the current query state, and its previous state, and contributes through learned additive residual updates. It does not overwrite the attention or multilayer-perceptron computations. The architecture was developed through two informative failures. FST v1 introduced a single formula slot but learned a partial-evidence shortcut. FST v2 imposed a strict two-path bottleneck, eliminating the shortcut but discarding useful partial evidence and limiting generalization. FST v3 instead retains distributed Transformer computation and adds a revisable side workspace. In a controlled modular rule-induction task, FST v3 was compared with a parameter-matched Transformer across ten paired random seeds. FST v3 used 582,870 parameters, compared with 584,915 for the matched Transformer. It improved mean held-out accuracy from 45.32% to 59.65%, achieved a median accuracy of 57.59%, won 9 of 10 paired seeds, and reduced the frequency of runs below 30% accuracy from 20% to 0%. The paired mean improvement was 14.34 percentage points, with a 100,000-sample paired-bootstrap 95% interval of 4.39 to 26.32 percentage points. Causal interventions indicate that the workspace is actively and input-specifically used. Disabling the workspace reduced mean accuracy to 16.99%. Cross-sample workspace permutation reduced it to 15.62%, while reversing the workspace contribution reduced it to 5.13%. Continuous workspace scaling produced a saturating dose-response curve, with performance improving from 16.99% at zero workspace strength to 59.42% at the trained scale and declining slightly when over-scaled. To test transfer beyond the synthetic rule task, FST v3 was adapted to character-level language modeling on a 10,008,096-character classical Chinese corpus. Across three seeds, FST v3 achieved 7.1979 test bits per character, compared with 7.2135 for a parameter-matched Transformer. This is an aggregate improvement of 0.0156 BPC, or approximately 0.216%. Disabling, permuting, or reversing the language-model workspace produced substantial degradation. However, the reference implementation required approximately 44% more training time, and the lower BPC did not yet produce a clear qualitative improvement in long-form free generation. The deposited package includes: - the preprint in PDF and editable DOCX formats;- complete FST v1, FST v2, and FST v3 implementation code;- complete ten-seed controlled-experiment outputs;- paired-bootstrap and merge-analysis code;- workspace disabling, permutation, reversal, and dose-response results;- the exact 10-million-character JSONL dataset;- parameter-matched Transformer and FST v3 language-modeling code;- complete three-seed language-modeling outputs;- publication figures;- release notes and citation metadata;- a file-level SHA-256 manifest. The current evidence supports FST v3 as a promising small-scale architectural prototype. It does not establish FST v3 as a general replacement for the Transformer. The principal limitations are the use of one primary synthetic task, small models, only three language-modeling seeds, increased training cost, distribution shift under workspace ablation, and the absence of large pretrained-model or long-form generation validation. Zhongren Wang conceived DP-SIT v2, proposed the formula-fusion hypothesis, directed the experimental questions, evaluated the theoretical implications, and assumes responsibility for the final manuscript and deposited materials. OpenAI Codex assisted with experimental-design refinement, code implementation, execution and verification of experiments, result aggregation and visualization, manuscript drafting and formatting, and construction and integrity checking of the reproducibility package. The AI system is not listed as an author. Author: Zhongren WangVersion: 1.0.0Release date: 28 August 2026Status: Experimental architecture preprint with complete reproducibility package

title: Zero-shot cross-lingual performance of multilingual models on XTREME-M with code generation versus NLU intermediate tasks
abstract: Zero-shot cross-lingual knowledge transfer enables the multilingual pretrained language model (mPLM), finetuned on a task in one language, make predictions for this task in other languages. While being broadly studied for natural language understanding tasks, the described setting is understudied for generation. title: 基于多体量子纠缠的超导量子计算
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to superconducting quantum computing based on multi-body quantum entanglement. Traditional superconducting quantum computing architectures largely rely on single-qubit entanglement, which presents significant challenges for scalability and complex quantum computations. This work proposes leveraging the unique properties of multi-body entanglement within specially designed superconducting circuits to overcome these limitations. We detail the theoretical framework underpinning this approach, focusing on the design principles for inducing and controlling multi-body entanglement, and outlining the potential for utilizing these entangled states for quantum information processing and storage. The core claim of this research is the construction of a scalable superconducting quantum computing platform by exploiting the effects of multi-body quantum entanglement. This represents a significant departure from conventional methods and offers a promising pathway towards realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Adaptive Noise Injection for Robust Training of Deep Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to training deep neural networks – adaptive noise injection – designed to enhance robustness and generalization performance. Traditional regularization techniques often employ fixed noise levels, which may be overly aggressive or insufficient depending on the specific training dynamics. Our method dynamically adjusts the noise level based on the network's learning progress, specifically monitoring gradient statistics. The core mechanism involves injecting noise into the training process proportionally to the magnitude of the gradient. This allows the network to adapt to varying levels of difficulty during training, mitigating the risk of overfitting and improving generalization to unseen data. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the methodology, that this adaptive approach offers a potentially more effective strategy compared to static regularization. The key equation representing the noise injection process is: Δst = η * (∂L/∂st) / ||∂L/∂st||, where Δst is the noise added at time step *t*, η is the scaling factor, ∂L/∂st is the gradient of the loss function L with respect to the parameter st, and ||∂L/∂st|| is the Euclidean norm of the gradient. This equation highlights the proportional relationship between the injected noise and the gradient magnitude. The paper details the implementation and provides a comprehensive explanation of the adaptive noise injection technique.

title: On Information-Theoretic Program Code Compression
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program code compression based on information theory principles. The core idea is to treat program code as an information sequence and apply techniques derived from entropy coding and redundancy reduction. Unlike traditional code compression methods that rely on statistical modeling of code patterns, this approach leverages the inherent statistical properties of code sequences, offering the potential for higher compression ratios, particularly for code with minimal redundancy. We explore the theoretical foundations of this method, focusing on the application of entropy estimation and optimized coding schemes. The presented framework aims to achieve efficient storage and transmission of program code by directly minimizing the information content, guided by the principles of information theory. The effectiveness of the method is discussed conceptually, without empirical validation through experimental results.

title: Histological Analysis of Zoonotic Diseases and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Zoonotic diseases remain major global public health challenges, requiring rapid, accurate, and scalable diagnostic approaches. Histological tissue analysis is fundamental for identifying the pathological features of zoonotic infections, but manual microscopy is limited by low throughput, observer variability, and shortages of specialist expertise. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning-based image analysis, is transforming the histological diagnosis of zoonotic diseases such as tuberculosis, brucellosis, and leishmaniasis within the One Health framework. It evaluates AI models for histopathological and cytological image analysis, explores applications in cross-species surveillance and geospatial disease monitoring, and discusses challenges related to implementation, explainability, and clinical adoption. The chapter concludes by outlining future directions for standardized, transparent, and accessible AI-driven veterinary histopathology.

title: Artificial Intelligence Maturity in Back-of-House Hotel Operations: Developing the AIM-BoH Framework Through a Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the hospitality industry at an unprecedented pace. However, existing hospitality research has overwhelmingly concentrated on customer-facing applications, including service robots, chatbots, personalization, and revenue management, while largely overlooking the internal operational systems that sustain hotel performance. As a result, the concept of AI maturity within back-of-house hotel operations remains theoretically undefined, fragmented across functional domains, and lacks an integrated framework for assessment. This study addresses this critical gap by asking a fundamental research question: What does AI maturity actually mean for hotel back-of-house operations? Drawing upon a systematic literature review following the PRISMA protocol, this study synthesizes evidence from 18 studies spanning the interdisciplinary fields of hospitality management, operations management, information systems, and artificial intelligence to examine how AI is transforming core internal hotel functions. The review identifies current applications, implementation patterns, organizational enablers, barriers to adoption, and emerging trends across human resource management, procurement, finance and accounting, inventory management, housekeeping planning, maintenance, energy management, and managerial decision support. Building on these findings, the study develops the Artificial Intelligence Maturity in Back-of-House Operations (AIM-BoH) Framework, a domain-specific conceptual framework designed to conceptualize AI maturity across hotel back-of-house functions. The framework conceptualizes AI maturity as a multidimensional organizational capability encompassing technological adoption, process automation, decision intelligence, data readiness, human–AI collaboration, governance and ethical preparedness, and measurable operational outcomes. By moving beyond technology-centric perspectives, the framework provides a comprehensive model for understanding how AI creates organizational value through the integration of internal hotel processes. The proposed framework advances hospitality literature by establishing a common theoretical foundation for understanding AI maturity in internal hotel operations while offering hotel executives a structured conceptual lens for considering organizational capability development in the planning of digital transformation initiatives. The article concludes by proposing a research agenda for the empirical validation, refinement, and cross-cultural application of the AIM-BoH Framework, positioning it as a reference model for future hospitality AI research and practice.

title: Generative AI as a Scaffold in Travel Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework
abstract: Tourism decision-making is cognitively demanding. Travelers navigate fragmented information, coordinate interdependent choices amid uncertainty, and sustain planning. Although generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in travel decision-making, tourism research has not explained how it alters the cognitive organization of decision-making. This article presents a framework theorizing generative AI as a scaffold across travel decision-making. The framework encompasses three pathways: mitigating executive load by structuring information and managing task-related demands; supporting psychological processing balance across intuitive, deliberate, and reflective modes; and sustaining decision continuity across iterative planning cycles. Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) tendencies serve as a theory-revealing case, where pronounced variation in executive function brings mechanisms into sharp relief. Grounded in task-based interviews with 30 UK adults, the framework extends tourism decision-making theory by explaining how generative AI redistributes cognitive work between travelers and digital systems and reorients AI design from efficiency optimization toward individualized cognitive and emotional support. Also available in Korean and Bahasa Indonesia.

title: Quantum Fourier transform toolbox
abstract: Quantum Fourier transforms (QFTs) are essential primitives in quantum algorithms. While abelian groups admit efficient QFT circuits, with circuit size polynomial in the logarithm of the group order, efficient constructions are known for relatively few non-abelian families. We develop two new approaches to QFT circuit construction, based on Mackey theory and Clifford theory, respectively, and use them to show exponential improvement in circuit cost for specific group families. Using the Mackey-theoretic approach, we obtain explicit quantum circuits for the QFT over $\mathrm{GL}_2(F_q)$ that scale polynomially in $\log q$, rather than polynomially in $q$. Using the Clifford-theoretic approach, we obtain QFT circuits for wreath products $F\wr S_n$, whose cost depends on the cost of a QFT over $F$ and the size of its representation registers. This removes the restriction $|F|=\operatorname{poly}(n)$ required by previous generic constructions and can yield exponential improvements when $F$ itself has an efficient QFT. Together, these methods provide new systematic tools to construct QFTs for broad classes of finite groups.

title: Composition without a Host: Carrying the Spatiotemporal-Composability Guarantee of Plugin-Based Agents across Processes
abstract: Plugin-based agents assemble capabilities at runtime, and the spatiotemporal-composability calculus proves a reversibility guarantee for this assembly. However, the guarantee is carried by a single process, which confines all components, sessions, and recovery records to one failure domain, where a fault spreads past the plugin boundary, and process death interrupts every session the process hosts. Resting only on the hypotheses the calculus already states and the stateless interface of the model call, this paper relaxes the single-process restriction of the calculus to an arbitrary assignment of components and records to processes, gives four sufficient conditions, and proves with Theorem 1, derived from the four lemmas, that the reversibility guarantee holds across processes when these conditions are met. Based on Theorem 1, this paper constructs Logos, a cross-process plugin-based agent in the peer-process and name-routed form of ROS, where a plugin is a process, the router holds only a rebuildable routing table, and the session state needed for recovery lives in an append-only transcript owned by no process. Under one fault on two hundred benchmark tasks across three configurations, the single-process reference lost every session and scored 1.5 percent on the official validator, the MCP configuration kept its sessions while spending 1099 calls on a dead endpoint, and Logos kept every session alive, wasted zero calls, and succeeded on 120 tasks against 102 for both configurations combined. At the mechanism level, eighty sessions terminated at four points of the tool-call cycle all resumed with no repeated action, 3,500 concurrent calls paired with zero violations, and one bus hop cost 1 in 823 of the model's first token. The results show that the reversibility guarantee holds across processes and that assembly itself can leave the host process.

title: Stability-Aware and Feasibility-Sensitive Aggregation in Federated Reinforcement Learning for Edge-IoT Systems: A Review
abstract: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a useful basis for distributed policy learning in Edge-IoT systems, where clients interact with local environments without transferring raw operational data to a central server. Yet aggregation becomes difficult when clients operate under different transition dynamics, workloads, resource capacities, communication conditions, and operational constraints. In these settings, local policy updates may not differ only in magnitude or direction; they may also differ in stability, reliability, resource support, and operational feasibility. Conventional averaging is therefore limited, since it does not distinguish stable and feasible updates from unstable or constraint-violating ones. This paper examines aggregation stability and feasibility-sensitive aggregation in FRL for Edge-IoT systems. It reviews and synthesizes related literature across four connected streams: heterogeneous Federated Learning, FRL-based edge decision-making, constrained and safe Reinforcement Learning, and adaptive or reliability-aware aggregation. The reviewed studies are analyzed through six dimensions: learning paradigm, type of heterogeneity, role of policy learning, treatment of operational constraints, aggregation strategy, and whether local feasibility signals influence global aggregation weights. The analysis indicates that existing studies provide valuable foundations, but they usually treat heterogeneity, constraint handling, and aggregation adaptation as separate concerns. The paper identifies a need for aggregation mechanisms that jointly account for update stability, update reliability, resource availability, and constraint feasibility. It positions aggregation as adaptive client influence regulation rather than passive averaging in future Edge-IoT FRL systems.

title: Fusing Transformer-Based Contextual Embeddings with Structured Semantic Knowledge for Improved Word Sense Disambiguation in Natural Language Processing
abstract: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that aims to determine the intended meaning of ambiguous words based on their contextual usage. Although Transformer-based language models have significantly improved contextual understanding, their decision-making process often lacks semantic transparency and explainability. Conversely, knowledge-based approaches leverage lexical databases and ontological resources to provide interpretable semantic relationships but are constrained by limited adaptability to diverse linguistic contexts. This research introduces a hybrid WSD framework that combines contextual representations generated by Transformer architectures with structured semantic knowledge extracted from ontology-driven repositories. By integrating contextual embeddings with knowledge embeddings, the proposed model enhances both contextual sensitivity and semantic consistency during the sense prediction process. The knowledge infusion mechanism enables the model to validate contextual interpretations using explicit semantic relationships, thereby improving the reliability of word sense assignments. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves superior performance compared with standalone contextual and knowledge-based approaches, yielding statistically significant improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score. The results indicate that combining deep contextual learning with structured semantic knowledge provides a robust and interpretable solution for accurate word sense disambiguation across diverse linguistic scenarios

title: A Phenomenological Information-Theory Framework for Large Language Models: A Unified Description of Memory, Forgetting, and Compression
abstract: This work constructs a unified phenomenological framework for memory and forgetting in large language models from fundamental quantities of information theory. The information-processing behaviours during training and inference are fully characterised by four primitives: mutual information, conditional entropy, the rate-distortion function, and noise. Memory is defined as a time-lagged mutual-information function linking the current system state to past inputs. Forgetting is described as the irreversible growth of conditional entropy over time. The strength of compression is measured by the slope of the rate-distortion curve. Within this framework, short-term and long-term memory form a single continuous spectrum, and semantic collapse emerges as a natural asymptotic behaviour in the rate-distortion limit. No external postulates are introduced; all constructs are derived from the axioms of information theory.

title: Meta-Learning for Domain Adaptation in Deep Learning
abstract: Domain adaptation is a crucial technique for addressing the problem of domain shift in deep learning, where models trained on one domain (source domain) perform poorly on a different domain (target domain). This paper explores the application of meta-learning to enhance domain adaptation capabilities in deep learning models. The core claim is that meta-learning provides a mechanism to train a meta-learner that can effectively adapt to new domains quickly. The proposed approach involves training a meta-learner to learn how to adapt, which is then utilized for domain adaptation. This method aims to improve the generalization performance of deep learning models across diverse domains. The paper outlines the framework, presents the underlying mathematical formulations, and discusses the potential impact of this approach.

title: VetHist-XAI
abstract: This study introduces the Veterinary Histology Explainable Transfer Framework (VetHist-XAI) that utilizes transfer learning from the EVA02 Vision Transformer (ViT) to automate binary classification of intestinal histopathology images into healthy vs. paratuberculosis-infected categories. Using a publicly available dataset of 366 H&E-stained tissue samples from sheep, goats, and cattle, we show that EVA02 fine-tuned with masked image modeling pretraining reports superior performance (accuracy: 0.9827±0.0135; MCC: 0.9649±0.0274) compared to conventional CNNs baselines (ResNet50, DenseNet121) and standard ViT architectures. VetHist-XAI incorporates robust validation via stratified 10-trial evaluation, comprehensive metric assessment including MCC for class-imbalance robustness, and explainable AI methods (LayerCam, GradCam++) to localize granulomatous lesions consistent with veterinary pathological expertise. Robustness analysis shows resilience to common imaging perturbations (e.g., brightness shifts, blur) while identifying specific vulnerabilities to high-frequency noise artifacts.

title: A Self-Similar Model of Type Theory
abstract: In this thesis we define a model of type theory parameterised by a self-similar action of a groupoid and a category. We begin by defining a new generalisation of algebraic theories internal to a type theory. We then define a new type theoretic generalisation of a category, which we call a weak-target category. We show that in the groupoid model of type theory weak-target categories are equivalent to self-similar actions of categories and groupoids. Additionally, we show weak-target categories in the groupoid model of type theory are equivalent to polynomial comonads on the category of groupoids. Finally, we show that the category of strict-presheaves over a weak-target category forms a model of type theory.

title: On the role of inductive bias in scaling quantum machine learning and variational quantum computing
abstract: The rapidly emerging paradigms of quantum machine learning (QML) and variational quantum computing (VQC) promise to combine quantum computational advantages with the powerful capabilities of machine learning and optimization. However, early attempts to naively translate classical machine learning techniques into the quantum domain have encountered severe scalability bottlenecks, both practical and theoretical. This dissertation posits that overcoming these limitations requires a fundamental shift in model and algorithm design: the deliberate integration of inductive bias. By embedding task-specific prior knowledge into quantum models and optimization strategies, this research demonstrates how to achieve the scalability required for near-term real-world applications and long-term success towards quantum advantage. This dissertation demonstrates the power of inductive bias across four methodological contributions. First, fast, gradient-free parameter and ansatz optimizers are developed to bypass costly gradient estimation on quantum computers. By explicitly embedding restriction and implicit biases into the quantum circuit ansatz and optimization method, these algorithms drastically improve resource efficiency, scaling variational quantum eigensolvers for molecular chemistry and quantum feature-map learning for classical data. Second, building on this scalable processing of high-dimensional classical data for discriminative tasks, the dissertation advances generative QML. To achieve high-quality, diverse real-world image generation, a quantum generator is designed with a strong, explicit inductive bias toward visual data, structurally reflecting both spatial image features and distribution characteristics. Third, complementary to learning from classical data, the dissertation advances QML for quantum data, processing inputs directly as quantum states rather than classical vectors. Here, a quantum Gaussian process paradigm is established, deriving a physics-informed inductive bias by encoding quantum information-theoretic assumptions. This bias guarantees provable model faithfulness and theoretical scalability. Finally, to ground this theoretical framework in physical reality, it is demonstrated on regression, classification, and optimization tasks, particularly for physical models. These physical applications close the loop to the initial quantum chemistry research, reinforcing both the overarching necessity and the natural presence of domain-specific inductive bias. Overall, the dissertation delivers timely and relevant findings that advance QML and VQC for near-term practical applications, while laying a foundation for the long-term perspective of quantum computing at scale.

title: A spatio-temporal graph attention association model for simulated multitarget tracking
abstract: Reliable online multi-target tracking requires associating noisy detections with existing tracks while preserving object identities through missed detections and clutter. This paper presents a simulation-based study of a spatio-temporal association model that combines an LSTM trajectory encoder, graph attention-based spatial context aggregation, a weighted binary association loss, a motion-prediction auxiliary head, distance-gated candidate generation, and global oneto-one online assignment. The evaluation uses five random seeds, an association score threshold of 0.3, and diagnostic analyses for gate/context threshold sensitivity, protocol exposure bias, motion-loss weighting, and component ablation under a unified online-history protocol. Across five seeds, the learned online model achieved MOTA = 0.7131 +/- 0.0461 and real-target recall = 0.8067 +/- 0.0527, while the constant-velocity Kalman filter with gated Hungarian assignment achieved MOTA = 0.7535 +/- 0.0552 and real-target recall = 0.8490 +/- 0.0629. The learned model therefore remains competitive on some seeds but does not consistently outperform the kinematic baseline. The discussion distinguishes supervised training pair accuracy from online tracking performance and identifies exposure bias, score calibration, class imbalance, and gate design as the main sources of the observed gap.

evidence.title: A spatio-temporal graph attention association model for simulated multitarget tracking
evidence.abstract: Reliable online multi-target tracking requires associating noisy detections with existing tracks while preserving object identities through missed detections and clutter. This paper presents a simulation-based study of a spatio-temporal association model that combines an LSTM trajectory encoder, graph attention-based spatial context aggregation, a weighted binary association loss, a motion-prediction auxiliary head, distance-gated candidate generation, and global oneto-one online assignment. The evaluation uses five random seeds, an association score threshold of 0.3, and diagnostic analyses for gate/context threshold sensitivity, protocol exposure bias, motion-loss weighting, and component ablation under a unified online-history protocol. Across five seeds, the learned online model achieved MOTA = 0.7131 +/- 0.0461 and real-target recall = 0.8067 +/- 0.0527, while the constant-velocity Kalman filter with gated Hungarian assignment achieved MOTA = 0.7535 +/- 0.0552 and real-target recall = 0.8490 +/- 0.0629. The learned model therefore remains competitive on some seeds but does not consistently outperform the kinematic baseline. The discussion distinguishes supervised training pair accuracy from online tracking performance and identifies exposure bias, score calibration, class imbalance, and gate design as the main sources of the observed gap.

title: ADNet: A multi-domain benchmark for anomaly detection across 380 real-world categories
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) aims to identify defects using normal-only training data. Existing anomaly detection benchmarks (e.g., MVTec-AD with 15 categories) cover only a narrow range of categories, limiting the evaluation of cross-context generalization and scalability. We introduce ADNet, a large-scale, multi-domain benchmark comprising 380 categories aggregated from 49 publicly available datasets across Electronics, Industry, Agrifood, Infrastructure, and Medical domains. The benchmark includes a total of 196,294 RGB images, consisting of 116,192 normal samples for training and 80,102 test images, of which 60,311 are anomalous. All images are standardized with MVTec-style pixel-level annotations, and anomalous samples are further enriched with structured text descriptions spanning both spatial and visual attributes, enabling multimodal anomaly detection tasks. Extensive experiments reveal a clear scalability challenge: existing state-of-the-art methods achieve 90.6% I-AUROC in one-for-one settings but drop to 78.5% when scaling to all 380 categories in a multi-class setting. To this end, we propose Dinomaly m , a context-guided Mixture-of-Experts extension of Dinomaly that forms image-conditioned decoder feed-forward networks through convex combinations of expert parameter banks. It achieves 83.2% I-AUROC and 93.1% P-AUROC, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining measured latency close to vanilla Dinomaly. We aim to make ADNet a standardized and extensible benchmark, supporting the community in expanding anomaly detection datasets across diverse domains and providing a scalable foundation for AD foundation models. Dataset: https://grainnet.github.io/ADNet .

title: Advancing Interaction-Sensitive Feature Selection: Novel Relief-Based Algorithms, Expanded Comparisons, and Recommendations for Biomedical Data Mining
abstract: As a precursor to high-dimensional biomedical data modeling, reliable feature selection can reduce computational expense, improve modeling performance, and yield simpler, more interpretable models. However, most filter-based feature selection methods struggle to detect feature interactions, while wrapper or embedded feature selection methods are computationally expensive. Relief-based algorithms (RBAs) are filter methods that are sensitive to feature interactions while mitigating these other limitations. This study (1) refactors, optimizes, and expands the scikit-rebate Python package with existing and newly proposed RBA variants and (2) conducts rigorous RBA benchmark comparisons across diverse genomic simulations. We expand scikit-rebate to include SWRF*, mu-Relief, and 5 novel RBA variants implementing alternative strategies for neighbor selection and feature scoring. All RBAs were evaluated to compare predictive feature ranking and runtime across simulated genomic datasets varying in sample size, number of features, heritability, and underlying association type (e.g. main effects and interactions). All RBAs, except mu-Relief, were proficient in detecting 2-way interactions in noisy data. RBAs utilizing 'far' scoring were best at detecting 2-way interactions - with MultiSWRFDB* top-performing - but were far less sensitive to main effects. SWRF, MultiSWRF, MultiSURF, and MultiSWRFDB yielded top performance across main effect and 2-way interaction datasets with MultiSWRFDB performing best when also considering 3-way interactions. Refactoring of scikit-rebate resulted in 10 to 35-fold reductions in RBA runtimes. The newly introduced RBAs were among the strongest performing, and by robustly retaining both main effects and 2-way epistatic interactions, these algorithms preserve predictive signals for downstream modeling.

title: Formal Verification of Program Code with Adaptive Strategies Based on Simulated Annealing
abstract: This paper explores the application of Simulated Annealing (SA) to the adaptive optimization of strategies for program code formal verification. Traditional formal verification methods often rely on predefined rules and heuristics, which may not be optimal for all programs. This research proposes a novel approach where SA is employed to dynamically adjust the parameters of the verification strategy, such as abstraction level and state space search range. The algorithm iteratively explores the parameter space, accepting changes that improve verification efficiency and coverage, while occasionally accepting changes that worsen the outcome to escape local optima. The core claim is that this adaptive strategy, driven by SA, significantly enhances the verification process. The formalization of this process through code, combined with the inherent exploration capabilities of SA, offers a flexible and powerful method for tackling complex verification challenges. The presented approach avoids the rigidity of rule-based systems, demonstrating improved performance and coverage rates. ---

title: Neuro-Symbolic Theorem Proving with Temporal Logic
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neuro-symbolic theorem prover designed to address the limitations of existing systems regarding temporal reasoning. The core concept involves integrating neural networks for pattern recognition with symbolic logic, specifically temporal logic, to represent and reason about events evolving over time. The system aims to bridge the gap between the strengths of neural networks – pattern detection and learning – and the rigorousness of symbolic logic – formal proof and deduction. The proposed architecture utilizes temporal logic to define constraints and dependencies between events, enabling the prover to systematically derive theorems involving temporal relationships. This extension significantly expands the problem domain for neuro-symbolic theorem proving, offering a pathway to more sophisticated reasoning capabilities. The system's ability to handle temporal aspects is crucial for applications in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems, and verification of reactive systems where understanding and reasoning about sequences of events is paramount.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) aims to train agents to make optimal decisions within an environment. However, many RL algorithms struggle to effectively balance exploration – trying new actions to discover rewards – and exploitation – using known actions to maximize rewards. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) within a probabilistic programming framework to address this challenge. The core idea is to learn the structure and parameters of the DBN adaptively based on the agent's experiences, thereby creating a probabilistic model of the environment's dynamics. This allows for more robust and flexible decision-making. The learned DBN acts as a prior for the agent's policy, guiding exploration and exploitation effectively. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and potential benefits. The resulting system offers a more principled way to handle uncertainty and adapt to complex, dynamic environments, potentially leading to improved performance in challenging RL tasks. ---

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes Based Computation Resource Allocation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to computation resource allocation leveraging the inherent error-correcting capabilities of quantum error correction (QEC) codes. Traditional approaches to resource allocation often struggle with the inherent noise and fragility of quantum systems, leading to inefficiencies and unreliable computations. Our proposed framework addresses this challenge by directly utilizing QEC codes to manage and allocate quantum computational resources. We decompose complex computational tasks into smaller, manageable units, encoded across multiple qubits using a chosen QEC code. The code's ability to detect and correct errors enables a robust and adaptive resource allocation strategy, dynamically adjusting the allocation based on observed error rates and resource utilization. This approach promises to significantly improve the utilization efficiency and reliability of quantum computing systems, particularly for complex and demanding computations. The core claim is the use of QEC's error correction capabilities to create an efficient computation resource allocation mechanism. The core mechanism involves task decomposition, error detection/correction, and dynamic adjustment based on resource utilization. This research offers a new paradigm for quantum resource management.

title: Temporal Logic Formalization for Quantum State Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces a novel temporal logic formalism, termed Temporal Quantum Logic (TQL), specifically tailored for representing and reasoning about the continuous evolution of quantum states. The core challenge in applying temporal logic to quantum mechanics lies in effectively capturing the inherent complexities of superposition, entanglement, and decoherence, particularly the non-commutativity of quantum operations. Existing temporal logics lack the necessary tools to accurately model these phenomena. TQL addresses this limitation by employing a multi-valued logic built upon tensor networks and process algebra concepts. This approach enables a precise and explicit representation of quantum operations, measurement outcomes, and their temporal dependencies, incorporating probabilistic semantics directly into the logic. The formalization utilizes a state representation based on tensor network contractions, allowing for the dynamic tracking of quantum state evolution over time. The logic incorporates operators that explicitly handle non-commutativity and decoherence, offering a framework for formally verifying the correctness of quantum algorithms and protocols. The key innovation is the combination of tensor network formalism with temporal logic, providing a rigorous method for describing the evolution of quantum systems and enabling a deeper understanding of their behavior. This work lays the foundation for future research in quantum verification, quantum algorithm design, and the development of quantum software.

title: Ontology-Driven Adaptive Learning Environment Using Large Language Models for Educational Knowledge Extraction
abstract: Enriching educational ontologies automatically from low-resource-language text remains an unsolved integration problem: conventional large language model (LLM)-to-knowledge-graph pipelines require a vocabulary-alignment step and lack hallucination control at the commit boundary. This study removes both bottlenecks and tests whether the resulting ontology can drive measurable learning gains. The core idea is schema co-design: the JSON schema constraining LLM output is the OWL T-box of the target ontology, so extracted records are directly populatable and no alignment step is needed; a literal-presence filter rejects entities absent from the source text before commit, the HermiT reasoner verifies consistency, and Kazakh, Russian and English labels are generated in a single follow-up call. The pipeline (Python 3.9, OWLready2) was benchmarked on 90 Kazakh paragraphs across GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro, and the resulting adaptive textbook was evaluated quasi-experimentally with 65 Grade 6 students (control n = 32, experimental n = 33) in two Astana schools over 16 weeks. Of 312 source chunks, 271 (86.9%) survived the full validation chain, yielding 1,847 OWL individuals, 2,931 object-property assertions and 6,512 data-property annotations across 47 classes; the literal-presence filter intercepted 5.2% of validated responses and the reasoner a further 1.1%. Extraction F1 reached 0.89 (GPT-4o), 0.87 (Claude) and 0.86 (Gemini), with hallucination rates of 4.9–8.3%; the one-time corpus build cost USD 3.47–9.64, with zero marginal LLM cost per learner. The experimental group outperformed controls on task accuracy (+19.4 points, d = 2.30), repeated errors (−53.6%, d = 1.85) and sessions to mastery (−34.3%, d = 1.50), all p < 0.001 under Bonferroni correction. The novelty lies in making the ontology T-box itself the extraction schema, combined with pre-commit literal grounding, validated in a real low-resource classroom deployment.

title: AI-Based Classification of Normal and Pathological Tissues
abstract: The modern landscape of veterinary medicine is in transition from traditional diagnostic techniques to advanced technological integration. A primary focus is placed on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning, which are increasingly used to automate medical imaging analysis, predict pregnancy outcomes, and enhance the accuracy of histopathological evaluations. The artificial intelligence details clinical case studies involving rare neoplasms, parasitic infections, and congenital abnormalities across dogs, cats, cattle, and exotic animals. Additionally, the oncology diagnosis examines the development of innovative diagnostic tools such as remote vital sensing, infrared spectroscopy, and bioelectrical impedance to improve animal welfare and surveillance. Research into molecular biomarkers and personalized oncology further illustrates the field's move toward high-precision, data-driven healthcare. This chapter explores clinical knowledge with emerging AI-based technologies for veterinary science and wildlife health.

title: Edge-Deployed Anomaly Indicators for UAV Telemetry with Context-Aware Advisory Decision Support
abstract: This paper presents a companion-computer chain that converts Pixhawk-class MAVLink telemetry into operator advice on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano. A twelve-channel sliding window (L=50, 10 s at 5 Hz) feeds a reference long short-term memory autoencoder and an edge-evaluated dense TensorFlow Lite model, which were trained with a session-level split of eight field sorties (train 14,429/validation 7281/test 6976 windows). Reconstruction mean squared error is mapped by validation-calibrated thresholds and a safe-inaction-first decision engine with K=3 action persistence. On a per-sortie fault-injection benchmark, One-Class SVM attains the highest pooled F1 score (0.713); the edge-evaluated dense TensorFlow Lite model reaches F1 0.524 (detector false-alarm rate 5.8%) at a 1.57 ms median on-device cost. Decision replay reports a 0.68% escalation false-alarm rate with the on-board gyro-x plausibility gate enabled, and 2.72% with the gate off. The study is a replay-profiled prototype on a single hexacopter; labelled evaluation uses synthetic injection, not concurrent live-load flight scoring.

title: XAI Integration in CI/CD
abstract: As AI-embedded software systems have evolved from academic research in laboratory set-ups to industry-specific real-time deployments, it is necessary to evolve XAI from post-analysis to continuous engineering practice. Integrating XAI into CI/CD pipeline ensures that each new model version not only gives accuracy assessment but also provides a transparent, auditable, and ethically viable solution throughout the model development lifecycle. Hence, this chapter focuses on how to integrate XAI in CI/CD pipeline of AI-based software systems development to provide continuous integration and continuous delivery of quality and trustworthy software systems.

title: SinkSLOT: Sinkhorn via Sparse Lifted Optimal Transport
abstract: Entropic optimal transport (EOT) has been shown to offer a computationally tractable approximation to exact optimal transport. However, the standard Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm has two main limitations. First, given discrete measures with $N$ points, each iteration requires $O(N^2)$ operations, which restricts its use on large-scale datasets (e.g. $N\geq10^4$). Second, it uses the independent coupling as a reference measure for regularisation. This assigns mass to high-cost transport edges at moderate regularisation strengths. We propose SinkSLOT, which addresses both limitations by putting forth the expected sliced lifted transport plan as a natural way to sparsify the Gibbs kernel with a non-independent prior coupling. We prove that: 1) SinkSLOT converges; 2) with $L$ slices, each resulting sparse Sinkhorn iteration costs $O(LN)$; and 3) the resulting objective is a divergence requiring no debiasing. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks show that SinkSLOT delivers substantial speedups over state-of-the-art dense and sparse EOT methods. We also demonstrate the applicability of the proposed divergence in a gradient flow experiment. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cai4cai/SinkSLOT.

title: GAN-Based Semantic Communication for Image Transmission in IoV
abstract: For cooperative perception in the internet of vehicles, this paper proposes a generative adversarial network-based semantic communication framework to address the efficiency and fidelity bottlenecks of traditional communication systems in visual data transmission under limited bandwidth and dynamic channel conditions. At the transmitter, the framework adopts a pyramid attention network to extract semantic label maps and introduces a semantic priority preservation mechanism. It assigns differentiated weights to distinct semantic categories based on driving safety, guiding bit allocation and loss function design. At the receiver, an image reconstruction module integrating a coarse to-fine multi-resolution generator and multi-scale discriminator is designed. Combined with the temporal consistency branch, spatial pyramid pooling and class-aware convolutional layers, it achieves high-fidelity reconstruction of high-quality images from corrupted semantic labels. The model is trained with combined adversarial, feature matching and perceptual losses, effectively improving semantic consistency and visual realism of generated images. Experimental results on the Cityscapes dataset show that the proposed method outperforms existing counterparts in both semantic segmentation accuracy and reconstructed image quality, and maintains stable reconstruction performance under AWGN and Rayleigh channels.

title: Online Differentially Private Consistent Clustering
abstract: We study differentially private (DP) $k$-means and $k$-median clustering in the online streaming setting. In this model, points arrive sequentially, and at each time step, we need to output a set of $k$ centers that optimizes the clustering objective for all points seen so far. We give a generic reduction that transforms the (sensitive) input stream into a private stream, which is a semi-coreset of the input stream. This implies that any (non-private) online clustering algorithm, run as a post-processing step, can achieve good utility for the original clustering objective. Our algorithm matches or improves upon the approximation ratio, space usage, and running time of existing algorithms [Epasto et al., 2026, Dupré la Tour et al., 2024]. A key aspect of our reduction is that it inherits desirable properties of the underlying non-private clustering algorithm, such as consistency [Lattanzi and Vassilvitskii, 2017]--a property not satisfied by previous DP algorithms.

title: Samudra Manthanam: Markup-Aligned Sanskrit–Russian Parallel Corpus of 148 Sources (corpus of record)
abstract: Markup-aligned parallel corpus of 148 sources (574,939 segment records), extracted deterministically from the source markup — in the source HTML the Sanskrit text and its Russian translation are interleaved as sibling blocks, and the converter reads the pairing directly; no statistical alignment is run. Composition: 119 verse sources (208,230 records), 15 dictionaries (321,672), 14 prose works (45,037). Headline: 78,219 clean 1:1 verse pairs (78,139 live re-count), plus 10,009 Russian-only and 80 Sanskrit-only monolingual segments. Includes 11 Russian translations of the Bhagavadgītā (1788–2015) with three commentaries — a built-in diachronic register set. Rights (per-layer): Sanskrit source text public domain by age; Russian translations pre-1930 editions public domain, 20th–21st-century editions in copyright with a grey residual, shipped under the project's standing ruling of 2026-08-08 with translators documented per source; imported DCS lemma/morphology layer CC BY 4.0 (Hellwig), redistributed with attribution; upstream code/schema/documentation Apache-2.0. The corpus texts carry their own rights and must be cited by their print editions; full table in the data statement file. Provenance: platform and converter at https://github.com/gasyoun/SamudraManthanam (software concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21317315 — cite that DOI for the software, this DOI for the corpus). Post-report upstream additions (121 files / 199,379 records) are excluded from this corpus of record and may appear in a future separately-versioned release. Corpus of record is byte-stable across four re-counts (2026-06-26, 2026-07-08, 2026-07-11, 2026-08-10); every figure recomputes in one deterministic pass.

title: Based on Neural Symbolic Reasoning for Program Formal Verification
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program formal verification by integrating neural symbolic reasoning. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both neural networks and symbolic logic to automate the process of program formalization and verification. Traditional formal verification methods are often hampered by the need for extensive manual definition of logical rules and constraints, leading to inefficiency and limited scalability. Our proposed framework addresses these limitations by employing neural networks to learn abstract representations of program code and combining them with symbolic logic for automated reasoning. Specifically, the system automatically generates formal specifications based on the learned representations and then utilizes a neural network to verify the specifications. This approach significantly reduces the manual effort involved in formal verification and offers the potential for increased efficiency and scalability. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a detailed description of the methodology and a conceptual framework. ---

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental quantum phenomenon, holds the potential for revolutionary information encoding techniques. This paper explores the utilization of quantum entanglement for secure data transmission and the development of a novel protocol, termed Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based on entangled states, aiming to surpass traditional cryptographic methods. The core mechanism centers around establishing a secure key distribution protocol leveraging the unique properties of entanglement. This research investigates the potential of this approach, focusing on the practical implementation and security analysis of the quantum entanglement encoding process. We will outline the theoretical underpinnings, design considerations, and preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of this new approach. This paper presents a comprehensive assessment of the potential benefits and challenges associated with this paradigm shift in information security.

title: Quantum Communication Protocol Based on Quantum Coherence Decay
abstract: This paper proposes a novel communication protocol leveraging the principles of quantum coherence decay for enhanced security. The core idea is to utilize the inherent fragility of quantum coherence – the tendency of a quantum system to lose its superposition and entanglement – to both protect and encrypt quantum information during transmission. The protocol utilizes a specific measurement strategy designed to exploit the decay of coherence, introducing a level of uncertainty that significantly increases the difficulty for eavesdroppers to intercept and reconstruct the transmitted information. Mathematical formalism is presented to describe the key aspects of the protocol, including the encoding scheme based on coherent state manipulation and the measurement process designed to detect and mitigate decoherence. The proposed approach represents a significant advancement in quantum communication security by directly addressing the fundamental vulnerability of quantum states to environmental noise. The protocol's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis, highlighting the potential for creating secure quantum communication channels.

title: Kraft–McMillan Equality: Conservation Law for Complete Prefix-Free Codes — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: The Kraft–McMillan inequality is the exact boundary condition for uniquely decodable codes, and its equality case corresponds to complete (maximally compact) prefix-free codes — a discrete analogue of a conservation law. | MATH: For a D-ary code with codeword lengths \(l_i\), the inequality is \(\sum_i D^{-l_i} \le 1\). Equality \(\sum_i D^{-l_i} = 1\) holds iff the code is *complete* (no unused leaves in the D-ary tree). For \(D=2\), the equality can be rewritten as \(\sum_i 2^{-l_i} = 1\). The golden ratio appears when \(D = \phi^2 = 2.618...\) (or \(D = \phi\) with a non-integer alphabet), giving \(\sum_i \phi^{-2l_i} = 1\) — a self-similar, fractal Kraft sum. The paper on permutation codes generalizes this to \(\sum_{\pi} \prod_{i} q_i^{l_i(\pi)} \le 1\) for non-uniform letter probabilities \(q_i\), with equality for complete permutation codes. | CONNECTION: The equality case \(\sum_i D^{-l_i} = 1\) is a **discrete harmonic balance** — the tree's leaf measure sums to unity Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Distributed Algorithm Design Based on Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the design and optimization of distributed algorithms utilizing multi-agent systems (MAS). The core claim is that MAS provide a framework for robust and adaptable algorithm design by leveraging distributed computation and interaction. The proposed mechanism involves decomposing algorithms into sub-tasks, assigning these to individual agents within the system, and facilitating collaboration and competition among them. This approach contrasts with traditional algorithm design methods which often rely on monolithic algorithms lacking inherent robustness. Through the utilization of MAS, this research aims to demonstrate a more efficient and reliable approach to algorithm design, particularly in scenarios demanding adaptability to changing environments and uncertainties. The paper outlines a general methodology for MAS-based algorithm design, focusing on the key aspects of agent communication, task allocation, and convergence analysis. The presented framework offers a significant advancement in distributed problem-solving by capitalizing on the inherent parallelism and fault tolerance characteristics of multi-agent systems. ---

title: Predictive Coding with Sparse Latent Representations and Temporal Context
abstract: This paper introduces a novel predictive coding framework designed to address limitations in existing models regarding temporal dependency capture and sparse representation learning. The core idea is to integrate sparse autoencoders for efficient low-dimensional latent representation learning with a recurrent neural network to explicitly model temporal context and facilitate future state prediction. The architecture leverages the predictive coding paradigm, where a generative model predicts the sensory input, and the prediction error drives updates. However, unlike traditional predictive coding, this framework employs sparse representations learned through autoencoders, resulting in more efficient and potentially more robust representations of the data. The recurrent neural network adds temporal context, allowing the model to learn predictive relationships across time steps. This approach is expected to improve the model's ability to handle sequential data and capture more complex temporal dynamics compared to models lacking these features. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail the architecture and the core equations governing the predictive coding process, sparse representation learning, and temporal context modeling.

title: Intermediate Task Training and Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Robustness in AmericasNLI Models
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does the inclusion of intermediate task training (e.g., NLI, QA) during fine-tuning affect the robustness of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual models for semantic understanding tasks in the AmericasNLI benchmark? title: AI-Supported Histological and Molecular Data Integration in Veterinary Sciences
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported integration of histological and molecular data has become an important innovation in veterinary sciences, enabling comprehensive multimodal analyses for disease diagnosis, biomarker discovery, and clinical decision-making. By combining digital histopathology with molecular datasets such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, AI can identify complex biological patterns that may not be detected through conventional approaches. Machine learning and deep learning algorithms improve tissue classification, lesion detection, prognostic assessment, and treatment monitoring with high accuracy and reproducibility. Furthermore, multimodal data integration facilitates the discovery of novel biomarkers associated with infectious, metabolic, and neoplastic diseases in animals. These advances contribute to the development of precision veterinary medicine by supporting early diagnosis, personalized therapeutic strategies, and more effective animal health management.
