title: Governing synthetic biology and artificial intelligence (AI) convergence: emerging biosecurity priorities for Africa
abstract: The rapid convergence of synthetic biology and artificial intelligence is reshaping the biosecurity landscape, yet governance approaches have not kept pace with the realities of digitally mediated biological research, particularly in African contexts. Existing global discourse has largely centred on high-level frameworks and treaty-based mechanisms, with comparatively less attention to how governance is operationalised within institutional systems. This paper addresses this gap by introducing and discussing structural exposure points defined here as systemic governance conditions that increase the likelihood that emerging technological capabilities will outpace oversight. Through an analysis of African biosafety regulatory bodies and national frameworks, the study identifies key exposure points, including fragmented institutional mandates, uneven regulatory and technical capacity, dependence on external technological infrastructure and limited integration of AI literacy within biosafety and biosecurity systems. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a set of pragmatic and context-sensitive governance priorities, including embedding AI considerations within existing biosafety and research review processes, adopting proportionate risk-based oversight approaches, strengthening cross-disciplinary capacity and establishing baseline expectations for DNA synthesis screening. It further advances an adaptive governance approach centred on training key personnel, integrating knowledge across institutional systems, strengthening coordination functions and enabling continuous policy learning through feedback. By shifting the focus from regulatory expansion to institutional integration, this paper intends to offer a feasible pathway for strengthening biosecurity governance in Africa hence helping support responsible scientific innovation while addressing the evolving risks of bio-digital convergence.

title: Physics-Guided Flow Matching for CT Image Reconstruction
abstract: Deep generative models have recently emerged as powerful priors for solving ill-posed inverse problems in CT, with diffusion-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance. However, diffusion models typically rely on stochastic sampling procedures, long inference trajectories, and carefully tuned noise schedules, which can limit computational efficiency and numerical stability, especially at high spatial resolutions. In this work, we investigate Flow Matching as an alternative generative prior for CT reconstruction. We train a high-resolution Rectified Flow Matching model on 256x256 chest images from the Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT dataset. To mitigate overfitting and limited anatomical variability, we employ a two-stage training strategy consisting of an initial phase with strong, anatomically informed data augmentation, followed by a fine-tuning phase with reduced or no augmentation to refine structural fidelity. The resulting model is capable of generating high-quality and anatomically coherent CT-like images, serving as a strong learned prior. title: Observability Analysis for Fusion of Doppler Measurements in Multistatic Radar Near the Tx-Rx Baseline
abstract: This paper studies multistatic measurement fusion when a target lies within the Tx--Rx (Transmitter-Receiver) baseline ambiguity zone, with particular emphasis on configurations involving two closely spaced stationary Tx--Rx pairs. Such configurations provide overlapping detectable regions and extend the effective detection range compared with sparsely spaced multistatic systems. However, in this region, the accuracy of range and bearing measurements degrades rapidly, and Doppler measurements often remain the only reliable information source. As a result, target trajectory estimation becomes highly challenging, with observability being marginal or even completely lost. To address this problem, the observability of target trajectories is analyzed under various conditions, enabling system designers to assess system performance in advance. A Doppler-only measurement fusion approach is then developed, employing a multiple-initial-point Maximum Likelihood (ML) nonlinear estimator for initial state estimation, followed by dynamic state updates using an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). Simulation results are presented and shown to be consistent with the observability analysis.

title: Future of Artificial Intelligence for Science in Japan 2024 Community Report
abstract: This white paper summarizes scientific challenges and AI/ML research opportunities identified through the FAIRS Japan 2024 unconference process. The discussion focuses on three major physics domains: accelerator physics, cosmology and astrophysics, and neutrino physics. Although each domain has distinct scientific goals and experimental constraints, several common technical themes emerge: high-dimensional reconstruction, fast and accurate simulation, uncertainty propagation, simulation-to-data mismatch, anomaly detection, real-time decision-making, and shared infrastructure.

title: Hybrid Batch Training Effects on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Inference Efficiency
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does hybrid batch training (mixing multilingual and English intermediate tasks) improve inference efficiency in zero-shot cross-lingual settings, as measured by latency-accuracy trade-offs on the XTREME benchmark? title: Emergent Formula States from Evidence Fusion in Transformers: A Controlled Test of DP-SIT v2
abstract: This record contains the preprint, complete experimental code, raw intervention-level outputs, derived evaluation tables, publication figures, software-environment information, reproducibility instructions, and a file-level SHA-256 manifest. The study tests whether two individually ambiguous evidence paths in a causal Transformer can coexist and form a new, non-additive hidden state that encodes an abstract rule and supports prediction on a held-out third case. The experiment is designed as a controlled test of Diagrammatic Path Expansion and State-Conditioned Signed Interference Theory (DP-SIT v2). A four-layer causal Transformer was evaluated under three matched training regimes: true-rule auxiliary supervision, no rule auxiliary supervision, and random-label auxiliary supervision. Each regime was trained for 4,000 optimization steps using three random seeds. In the primary no-auxiliary condition, the model achieved 50.21% mean held-out answer accuracy when both evidence paths were present, compared with 39.41% with one path and 18.31% with neither path. After the Transformer was frozen, an independently trained linear probe decoded the latent rule from the fusion-position hidden state with 99.91% held-out accuracy. Non-additive factorial interaction increased across residual-stream depth, while its relative share declined toward the final readout. These results support a state-conditioned fusion-and-selective-retention account: jointly available evidence can form a formula-readable hidden state, while downstream computation only partially retains and converts that state into the task-specific output. The current evidence does not establish that the decoded formula subspace is causally necessary, nor does it prove that the mechanism generalizes to pretrained language models or natural-language tasks. Formula-subspace ablation, state transplantation, edge-level mediation, alternative intervention baselines, additional random seeds, and cross-model replication remain necessary. The deposited package includes: - the preprint in PDF and DOCX formats;- complete training and intervention code;- raw JSON outputs for all reported conditions and random seeds;- per-seed, aggregate, and layerwise CSV tables;- publication figures;- one-command reproduction scripts;- environment and methodological documentation;- citation metadata;- a file-level SHA-256 manifest. title: Dynamic Topological Embedding Learning (T2L)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topological Embedding Learning (T2L), a novel approach to neural network learning that leverages dynamic topological structures for enhanced knowledge representation and reasoning. The core claim of T2L is that by adaptively adjusting the network's topology and embedding it into dynamic topological data, significantly improved efficiency and robustness can be achieved. The proposed mechanism utilizes network weights and connection weights as a topological network, employing optimization algorithms based on information bottleneck and topological consistency to iteratively adjust the network's node connections and weights, maximizing internal information flow and consistency with the input data's topology. A key innovation is the dynamic generation and modification of the network's topology, responding to data changes and learning objectives. Furthermore, a "topology memory" mechanism is integrated to preserve past topological features, bolstering the ability to model long-range dependencies. The results demonstrate T2L's capability to outperform traditional methods in scenarios involving complex, evolving data.

title: Quantum Error Correction and Compression via Topological Representations
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum error correction and compression leveraging the unique properties of topological quantum networks. We propose a new encoding scheme based on physical entanglement within the network, combined with topological protection mechanisms, to achieve robust quantum information transmission and storage. Furthermore, we introduce a topological compression algorithm to significantly reduce the redundancy inherent in traditional quantum error correction codes. Our method aims to overcome limitations of existing schemes by deeply integrating topological quantum mechanics with the fundamental physical principles of quantum error correction. The core of the approach relies on light-path encoding based on entanglement and utilizes topological protection to safeguard quantum information. The proposed compression algorithm actively removes redundant encoding information, leading to a substantial reduction in the overall code size. Simulation results demonstrate the potential of this combined approach for realizing efficient and scalable quantum communication and computation. The key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of physical entanglement and topological protection, offering a pathway to more practical quantum error correction and compression.

title: Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds on Neural Network Capacity
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to determining the theoretical lower bounds on the capacity of neural networks required for accurate function representation. We establish these bounds using information-theoretic concepts, specifically leveraging the channel capacity of the underlying representation space. Our methodology centers on quantifying the information needed to encode the function's output, ultimately providing a fundamental limit on network size that transcends empirical observations. The core contribution lies in deriving tight information-theoretic lower bounds, offering a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding and justifying neural network architecture choices. We explore the relationship between function complexity, the representation space's capacity, and the resulting network size, demonstrating how information theory provides a solid foundation for this analysis. The results presented here aim to move beyond the reliance on empirical scaling laws and offer a more robust and theoretically grounded approach to neural network design.

title: Dynamic Neural Networks with Memory-Augmented Attention
abstract: This paper proposes a novel dynamic neural network architecture designed to overcome the limitations of traditional networks in handling long-term dependencies. The core idea is to integrate a memory module with an attention mechanism, enabling the network to selectively attend to and retain pertinent information from its past experiences. We introduce a framework where the memory module acts as a temporal buffer, storing past states, and the attention mechanism dynamically weights the importance of these stored states when processing current inputs. This approach allows the network to learn and utilize complex temporal patterns more effectively. The architecture is formally defined with equations detailing the memory update rule, the attention weighting process, and the overall network flow. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance in tasks requiring long-range context understanding compared to standard recurrent neural networks. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of memory augmentation and attention, providing a robust solution for dynamic sequence modeling.

title: Attention-Driven Histopathology Segmentation and Classification Using Deep Learning
abstract: This chapter investigates the critical challenges impeding the global adoption of automated diagnostic systems in veterinary medicine and proposes a robust mathematical framework to resolve them. Traditional machine learning methodologies frequently fail when processing non-standardized biological data. Consequently, the authors detail a multi-stage deep learning pipeline leveraging an Attention-gated U-Net and DenseNet-121 architecture. This framework explicitly addresses laboratory-induced dye inconsistencies through rigorous optical density space normalization while simultaneously resolving the biological occlusion of malignant cells via dynamic spatial attention mechanisms. Furthermore, this chapter provides actionable solutions for clinical deployment, emphasizing human-in-the-loop workflows, post-training quantization for edge computing, and active learning ecosystems to mitigate extreme data scarcity, ultimately democratizing advanced diagnostic capabilities for diverse species.

title: A cross-platform study of near-term quantum optimisation algorithms on the graphene defect problem
abstract: Abstract Quantum computers show potential for achieving computational advantage over classical computers, with many candidate applications in combinatorial optimisation. We present a focussed, application-level hardware case study of near-term quantum optimisation algorithms applied to a dense quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation (QUBO) materials science problem. To solve this problem, we implement two methods, the variational quantum eigensolver and quantum annealing (QA), on commercially-available gate-based and QA devices that are accessible via Quantum-Computing-as-a-Service (QCaaS) models. To analyse the performance of these algorithms on our chosen problem, we use a toolbox of relevant metrics and compare performance against three classical algorithms. We employ quantum methods to solve our fully-connected QUBO of up to 72 variables, and find that algorithm performance beyond this is restricted by device connectivity, noise and classical computation time overheads. The classical method—simulated annealing—demonstrates the best performance, exhibiting polynomial scaling on the tested problem sizes.

title: Advancements in deep learning for early breast cancer detection using artificial intelligence models in low resource settings
abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of mortality among women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), compounded by fewer radiologists available and resources for diagnosis. A narrative review that summarizes 45 peer-reviewed publications to date from 2018 to 2025 is presented for deep learning (DL) models for mammography detection for breast cancer, targeting low-resource-critical architectures for development in LMIC settings. We compare convolutional neural networks (CNNs), hybrid CNN-support vector machine (SVM) models, recurrent/LSTM networks, and lightweight architectures such as MobileNet and EfficientNet. In quantitative synthesis the reported diagnostic accuracy for MobileNet is between 89 and 92%, supported with 128 MB RAM and 0.3 GFLOPs. Therefore it is appropriate for offline edge devices (smartphones, NVIDIA Jetson Nano). EfficientNet achieves 91–94% accuracy—though it requires stable internet to enable cloud deployment, due to its greater parameter size (5.3 million). Both architectures reduce false positives by 7 to 69% and false negatives by 9% compared to traditional computer-aided detection, though most evidence is retrospective. The most important contributions from this review are: (1) a quantitative comparison of efficiency for edge versus cloud deployment, (2) detection of dataset bias (no LMIC-specific validation exists), and (3) practical recommendations regarding infrastructure, regulatory pathways, and privacy-preserving federated learning. Limitations include cross-study heterogeneity in datasets (CBIS-DDSM, INbreast, MIAS) and evaluation protocols. We conclude that MobileNet and EfficientNet provide good trade-offs for LMICs but call for prospective trials and locally curated datasets before clinical implementation.

title: An Enclosed Mode Is a Gauge Choice: Topology Relative to Reach in Certified Code World Models
abstract: A code world model accepted by a sampling gate can be exactly right on everything the gate can see and arbitrarily wrong beyond it. We characterize what a certified model can know, and what its errors can cost, when the omission is an annular freeze mode enclosing an unreachable interior. The gate quotient makes the question precise: acceptance-with-certainty determines the model exactly on the reachable query set; beyond reach is gauge. On a minimal ring instrument we prove the extreme case (a wrong-topology filled-disc artifact unfalsifiable by any sampling gate and bitwise harmless at play) and measure, with LLM synthesis across three model families, how one knob (a channel of width gamma) walks the same artifact through three regimes: unfalsifiable-and-harmless, falsifiable-and-costly, and instantly falsified. Three principles organize the empirics. First, danger is topology relative to reach: a channel the planner can use collapses the blind model's exploitation (play cost 1.09 to ~0 over a knee at gamma ~ 0.1), while a hidden channel with the same first Betti number keeps it at full strength (1.12). Second, repair is parameter-bound and sensor-bound: no family recovers the region from outside evidence; from inside, models pose the right topology but cannot pin its parameters, and the posed topology tracks the guiding persistent-homology summary's wrong beta_1 (a sensor with a measured geometric resolution limit), not the truth. Third, mitigation must match the error's dimension and direction: point fences fail against the one-dimensional boundary, a dimension-matched persisted fence collapses exploitation to a two-lesson transient (0.999 to 0.058), and the dual freedom certificate collapses the invented-mode failure symmetrically (1.769 to 0.029). In n dimensions the shell makes misidentification near-certain while the danger stays fully exploitable: the two axes are independent.

title: Regime-Aware Portfolio Management via Retrieval-Augmented LLM-Guided Expert Switching
abstract: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, making the effectiveness of individual portfolio-management strategies highly dependent on changing market conditions. This work proposes a retrieval-augmented expert-switching framework that dynamically selects portfolio management experts based on their historical performance under similar market situations. A dual-stream variational autoencoder represents asset-level and market-wide information, while a retrieval-based knowledge base stores historical situations and expert performance. During inference, an instruction-tuned LLM reasons over the retrieved evidence to identify the most appropriate expert rather than directly generating portfolio actions. We further establish a monotonicity property showing that adding a locally superior expert cannot degrade the switching mechanism's performance. Experiments across cryptocurrency, stock, and foreign-exchange markets show that the proposed selector achieves the highest cumulative return and Sharpe ratio among the evaluated selection strategies in all three markets. In the stock market, for example, cumulative return increases from 26% for the best fixed expert to 34%, while the Sharpe ratio improves from 0.74 to 0.96. Ablation results confirm the importance of both retrieval and LLM reasoning, while experiments with different expert-pool sizes demonstrate the value of complementary expertise. Overall, the findings support retrieval-grounded expert switching as an effective approach to adaptive portfolio management in non-stationary financial environments.

During inference, an instruction-tuned LLM reasons over the retrieved evidence to identify the most appropriate expert rather than directly generating portfolio actions. We further establish a monotonicity property showing that adding a locally superior expert cannot degrade the switching mechanism's performance. Experiments across cryptocurrency, stock, and foreign-exchange markets show that the proposed selector achieves the highest cumulative return and Sharpe ratio among the evaluated selection strategies in all three markets. In the stock market, for example, cumulative return increases from 26% for the best fixed expert to 34%, while the Sharpe ratio improves from 0.74 to 0.96. Ablation results confirm the importance of both retrieval and LLM reasoning, while experiments with different expert-pool sizes demonstrate the value of complementary expertise. Overall, the findings support retrieval-grounded expert switching as an effective approach to adaptive portfolio management in non-stationary financial environments.

title: Contextualized Graph Attention Networks with Memory Augmentation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph representation learning that leverages the strengths of Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and Memory Networks. We propose a framework for Contextualized Graph Attention Networks with Memory Augmentation, which integrates a trainable recurrent memory module to enhance GATs' ability to capture long-range dependencies within graphs. The core claim is that augmenting GATs with contextual memory significantly improves their capacity to model complex relational dependencies. The proposed mechanism utilizes a memory module to store and retrieve past graph states, effectively enabling the network to 'remember' and utilize these long-range dependencies. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate that this approach outperforms standard GATs in scenarios requiring the understanding of intricate relational structures. The primary contributions of this work are a new architectural design and a rigorous evaluation demonstrating the benefits of memory augmentation for graph representation learning.

title: Quantum-Inspired Hardware-Aware Compiler Optimization
abstract: Traditional compiler optimization focuses on maximizing performance within the constraints of classical architectures. However, quantum computing presents a fundamentally different paradigm, demanding a new approach to software optimization. This paper proposes a hardware-aware compiler optimization technique, inspired by quantum computing principles, to bridge the gap between high-level programming languages and the specific characteristics of quantum hardware. The core idea is to translate high-level code into quantum circuits while explicitly considering factors like qubit connectivity, gate fidelity, and decoherence. This approach allows for optimization strategies tailored to the unique limitations and opportunities of quantum devices, potentially leading to significant performance improvements compared to generic quantum compilation methods. The compiler operates by analyzing the algorithmic complexity, identifying quantum-native operations, and strategically mapping them onto the available quantum hardware, thereby minimizing the impact of hardware constraints. This paper outlines the framework, key components, and potential optimizations within this hardware-aware compiler.

title: Meta-Learning for Reinforcement Learning of Complex Robotic Skills
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown remarkable success in various domains, but its application to complex robotic skills often faces significant challenges. Traditional RL methods typically require extensive training data and careful task-specific design, hindering their ability to generalize and transfer to new robotic tasks. This work proposes a meta-learning framework to address these limitations. The core idea is to train an RL agent to learn how to learn – essentially, equipping it with the ability to quickly adapt to novel robotic tasks with limited training samples. We leverage model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) and introduce a novel reward shaping function designed to accelerate the meta-learning process. Our approach demonstrates the potential for rapid skill acquisition in robotic systems, paving the way for more adaptable and efficient robotic learning.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks for Sensor Fusion
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-organizing neural networks to the problem of sensor fusion. Traditional sensor fusion techniques often rely on pre-defined architectures and manual tuning, which can be computationally expensive and may not adapt well to varying sensor data characteristics. We propose a novel approach utilizing a neural network architecture that dynamically adjusts its structure and connections through a reinforcement learning process. The network learns to effectively fuse data from multiple sensors by observing the input signals and optimizing its internal connections based on a defined reward function. This self-adaptive mechanism eliminates the need for manual architectural design, potentially leading to more robust and efficient sensor fusion systems. The core claim is that neural networks can learn to effectively fuse data from multiple sensors through a process of self-organization, adapting their architecture and connections based on the input data. The core mechanism involves a network architecture where connections are dynamically pruned and grown based on the relevance of the input signals, guided by a reinforcement learning objective.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Emergent Communication
abstract: This paper explores the phenomenon of emergent communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems. We investigate whether agents, when tasked with a shared goal within a MARL environment, can autonomously develop communication protocols without any pre-defined rules or instructions. The core claim is that reinforcement learning, through iterative interaction and reward maximization, can drive the emergence of sophisticated communication strategies. We present a framework for examining this process, focusing on the learning dynamics and the resulting communication patterns. The results demonstrate the potential for agents to learn to effectively coordinate their actions and exchange information, highlighting a key step towards truly intelligent multi-agent systems. This research contributes to the growing field of MARL and offers insights into how complex behaviors can arise from simple learning mechanisms. The study analyzes the impact of various environmental parameters on the emergence of communication, providing a foundational understanding for future research in this area.

title: AI in Veterinary Diagnostics
abstract: Veterinary histopathology is one of the major diagnostic, prognostic, and management tools in disease treatment, but the traditional approach to histopathological analysis meets numerous limitations, such as subjectivity, work intensiveness, observer variability, and limited access to qualified veterinarians. Digital pathology and artificial intelligence offer a novel approach to automated disease identification, classification, segmentation, and biomarker quantification in veterinary diagnosis. Moreover, artificial intelligence may contribute to the control of infectious and zoonotic diseases through lesion detection and confirmation. Nonetheless, efficient utilization of the approach in clinical practice requires numerous data sets, expert annotation, validation on multiple levels, comprehensible outputs, standardization of imaging, and proper governance.

title: Deep Learning-Based Anomaly Detection in Brain Magnetic Resonance Images
abstract: This paper investigates approaches to anomaly detection in high-dimensional data using modern deep learning techniques. Particular attention is devoted to the analysis of medical images, specifically brain MRI scans, as well as time series data characterized by complex structures and the presence of latent nonlinear dependencies. Data preprocessing methods and the specifics of training models on normal samples to construct a baseline distribution of typical data are examined. The study explores the applicability of variational autoencoders (VAE), generative adversarial networks (GAN), and transformer-based architectures for anomaly detection tasks. A comparative evaluation of these models is conducted using key performance metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score. Experimental results obtained on publicly available medical datasets demonstrate the advantages of transformer-based models in detecting pathological changes, while generative approaches prove effective for modeling the distribution of normal data and for training data augmentation. The obtained results confirm the feasibility of employing generative and transformer-based models for medical data analysis and highlight their potential for integration into intelligent clinical decision support systems. The main contribution of this study lies in a structured comparative analysis of VAE, GAN, and Transformer-based architectures under a unified experimental pipeline for anomaly detection in medical imaging data. The experimental setup is designed to ensure consistent evaluation across models using identical preprocessing procedures and evaluation metrics. In addition, the study provides a reproducible framework for assessing generative and attention-based models in the context of medical anomaly detection tasks.

title: Slice-Aware Adversarial Vulnerability Analysis of TabNet-Based Intrusion Detection in 5G Network Slicing
abstract: A TabNet-based network intrusion detection system can achieve 97% global accuracy while simultaneously exhibiting near-total adversarial collapse in the URLLC slice (PSRI = 0.023)—a critical vulnerability that conventional metrics entirely conceal. This paper introduces the Per-Slice Robustness Index (PSRI) and Slice-Weighted F1 (SW-F1) to expose such hidden vulnerabilities in 5G network slicing environments, and proposes Attention-Guided Evasion (AGE), a transfer-based adversarial attack that exploits TabNet’s native attention mask to concentrate perturbations on the most influential features. Using the CICIoT2023 dataset with 34 attack categories mapped to eMBB, URLLC, and mMTC service slices, we demonstrate that AGE achieves a 50.2% accuracy drop at ε=0.10 while using 17× less L2 perturbation than FGSM and modifying only 8.5% of features. The proposed metrics expose a 0.121-point gap between global weighted F1 (0.928) and slice-balanced SW-F1 (0.807), demonstrating that conventional evaluation systematically overestimates protection for minority slices in heterogeneous 5G environments. These findings highlight the necessity of slice-aware adversarial evaluation frameworks for 5G network security.

title: IPD of Multivariate Power Series Distributions
abstract: This chapter develops a unified theoretical framework for the distribution of squared IPDs within the broad class of multivariate power series distributions (MPSDs). Encompassing important models such as the multinomial, negative multinomial, multivariate Poisson, and multivariate logarithmic distributions, MPSDs provide a natural foundation for analyzing high-dimensional discrete and count data. The chapter derives explicit distributional results for IPDs under a variety of settings, including independent and non-identically distributed vectors, mixture models, and distances from fixed reference points. These results establish analytical tools for understanding IPD behavior in high dimensions. Building on these developments, the chapter formulates IPD -based tests of homogeneity for mixture models with both known and estimated parameters, complemented by bootstrap density estimation. Comparative studies demonstrate the effectiveness of IPD -based procedures relative to competing homogeneity tests, with applications ranging from synthetic mixtures to real data, including the Old Faithful geyser dataset. By providing closed-form expressions and rigorous proofs, this chapter underscores the central role of IPDs in high-dimensional inference, classification, clustering, and model discrimination for discrete multivariate data.

title: InstructMesh: Selective Refinement of Generative 3D Models for Fabrication
abstract: Recent advances in generative AI allow users to create 3D models from text or images. However, these models prioritize visual plausibility over geometric accuracy, often generating results with flaws that compromise their intended use post-fabrication. We present InstructMesh, an interactive post-generation refinement tool that enables selective repair of generative 3D models through region selection and targeted operations, such as opening or sealing voids, or adjusting local thickness. Users can invoke edit operations via natural language prompts or slider controls. By operating directly on the intermediate latent representation, InstructMesh allows users to apply robust geometric corrections without requiring expert modeling skills. To inform our design, we first analyze common fabrication-related failure modes in outputs from state-of-the-art generative tools. We then conduct two user studies, demonstrating that novices can identify and perform fabrication-relevant repairs on generative outputs using InstructMesh, and revealing user preference for hybrid interfaces that combine slider controls with natural language input.

title: Synth-JDoc: Synthesizing a Japanese Document Image Dataset for OCR with Diverse Layouts and Embedded Images
abstract: The ability of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) to read text within document images is crucial, as it enables various applications such as Document Visual Question Answering. To enhance the text-reading capabilities of LVLMs, high-quality OCR datasets are essential. This need is particularly critical for Japanese documents, which often feature vertically written text alongside horizontally written text. Current LVLMs demonstrate considerably lower performance on vertically written Japanese text than on horizontally written text, necessitating specialized OCR datasets to bridge this gap. However, manually constructing OCR datasets is expensive and difficult to scale. Alternatively, constructing datasets by extracting text from existing document images using OCR models introduces challenges, such as text recognition errors and the prerequisite of sourcing document images. To address these issues, we construct an OCR dataset by synthesizing document images directly from text. Leveraging HTML and CSS, we generate multi-column documents that incorporate both vertical and horizontal writing styles. Furthermore, to ensure the visual realism of the documents, we embed images generated by text-to-image models within the layout. Additionally, to foster model robustness, we apply noise and degradation filters to the synthesized document images. In our experiments, we compared the performance of models fine-tuned on our synthetic dataset against baselines fine-tuned on synthetic datasets from prior work and those generated by a high-performance text-to-image model. Evaluation results demonstrate that our synthetic dataset is the most effective approach for improving LVLM performance on reading vertically written Japanese text. Our dataset and code are publicly available (https://github.com/llm-jp/synth-jdoc).

title: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing Driven Adaptive Learning for Personalized GCE Examination Preparation
abstract: Examination preparation for the General Certificate of Education in Cameroon relies heavily on static past question booklets that treat every learner identically regardless of what that learner has already mastered. This paper reports the design, implementation, and simulation-based validation of a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-driven adaptive quiz engine built for GCE Ordinary Level Chemistry within the ToriLearn prototype platform. The engine estimates a learner's mastery of eleven syllabus-defined knowledge components after every response, using the canonical four-parameter Bayesian Knowledge Tracing formulation together with penalty adjustments for hint use, skipped questions, and viewed answers, and it feeds the resulting mastery estimate into a real-time decision engine that selects the next question's difficulty. We describe the mathematical formulation as implemented, the sequence of operations executed on every answer submission, and three synthetic learner scenarios constructed to test whether the engine's behaviour matches the behaviour the underlying model predicts. Results show that a consistently correct simulated learner reaches high mastery within a small number of attempts and is advanced to harder material, that a consistently incorrect learner is retained on remedial content without mastery collapsing to zero, and that a learner with alternating performance produces a fluctuating difficulty trajectory that tracks the fluctuating mastery estimate. The endpoint that performs this computation responded within 45 to 80 milliseconds under local development testing. No real student data were used to fit the model parameters and no classroom trial was conducted, so the contribution of this paper is a validated implementation of the Bayesian mechanism rather than measured evidence of examination performance improvement.

title: Data and Code for Quantum Machine Learning for Acoustic Signal Classification
abstract: This record contains the data, code, configuration files, result tables, and generated figures associated with the study “Quantum Machine Learning Methods for Acoustic Signal Classification.” The project evaluates near-term quantum machine learning methods for environmental sound classification using ESC-50 and UrbanSound8K. The included materials support reproducibility of the reported experiments comparing a convolutional neural network baseline, a quantum kernel support vector machine, and variational quantum classifiers. The record includes scripts for preprocessing, feature extraction, model training/evaluation, VQC ablation experiments, table generation, and confusion-matrix visualization. It also includes generated result files and figures used in the manuscript. The original ESC-50 and UrbanSound8K audio datasets are also included here.

title: Quantum-Walk Based Optimization of Neural Network Weights
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum walks for optimizing the weights within neural networks. Traditional neural network training relies heavily on classical gradient-based optimization methods, which can often get trapped in local minima and suffer from slow convergence rates. We propose a novel approach leveraging the inherent properties of quantum walks to efficiently explore the complex solution space of neural network weight optimization. The core idea involves mapping the weight update process to a quantum walk, where each walker represents a candidate weight adjustment. The walk's evolution is determined by a Hamiltonian operator constructed from the neural network's loss function. title: Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Circuits
abstract: This paper proposes and details the design of Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Circuits (APLCs), a novel computational system engineered to dynamically adjust its logic gates and circuit topology based on incoming data. The core concept leverages machine learning algorithms to train the parameters of the APLC, enabling it to autonomously select optimal logic gates and modify circuit connections for enhanced computational efficiency and accuracy. Traditional probabilistic logic circuits suffer from static design and a lack of adaptive capabilities. APLCs address this limitation by integrating self-learning mechanisms, resulting in a system capable of optimizing its structure during computation. This work outlines the architecture, learning process, and theoretical underpinnings of APLCs, presenting a foundational approach for more efficient probabilistic and fuzzy reasoning. The system's adaptive nature promises significant improvements in handling complex and evolving datasets, a key advantage over static probabilistic models. The primary goal is to move beyond fixed logic designs, allowing the circuit to respond to the nuances of the problem being solved.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis via Relational Logic Programming
abstract: The synthesis of executable programs from high-level specifications is a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches often rely solely on either neural networks or symbolic programming, each with inherent limitations. This paper presents a novel neuro-symbolic framework for program synthesis that aims to bridge the gap between these two paradigms. Our system utilizes neural networks for robust feature extraction and relational logic programming for the generation of executable code. A key innovation lies in the design of a specialized loss function that simultaneously optimizes the accuracy of both the neural and symbolic components. We demonstrate that this integrated approach can achieve significantly better performance compared to standalone neural or symbolic methods. The core claim of this work is that by combining the strengths of neural networks and relational logic programming, we can create a truly synergistic neuro-symbolic system. This research contributes to the broader field of AI by providing a new methodology for building intelligent systems capable of both learning and reasoning. The system's architecture facilitates a more flexible and interpretable program synthesis process.

title: Based on Differential Geometry: Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network optimization based on the principles of differential geometry. Traditional neural network training relies heavily on gradient-based methods, often struggling with challenges such as vanishing gradients, saddle points, and difficulties in navigating complex loss landscapes. We propose a framework that reformulates the neural network optimization problem as an optimization problem within the context of differential geometry. Specifically, we represent the neural network's loss function as a curvature field. By leveraging the concept of gradient flows associated with this curvature field, we can efficiently locate the minimum of the loss function. This approach offers a fundamentally different perspective, potentially overcoming limitations associated with conventional gradient descent methods. The core of this work lies in the transformation and subsequent geometric analysis of the loss function, providing a new pathway to stable and effective neural network training. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, paving the way for further investigation and development. ---

title: 基于深度学习的符号推理引擎 (Deep Learning-Based Symbolic Reasoning Engine - DLBRE)
abstract: This paper presents Deep Learning-Based Symbolic Reasoning Engine (DLBRE), a novel approach to symbolic reasoning leveraging the power of deep learning. The core claim is that deep learning models can be trained to perform symbolic reasoning, thereby unlocking more sophisticated capabilities for Artificial Intelligence. DLBRE transforms the symbolic reasoning process into a continuous optimization problem through a specifically designed deep neural network architecture. Unlike traditional symbolic reasoning engines that rely on manually crafted rules, DLBRE harnesses the self-learning capabilities of deep learning. This work explores the architecture of DLBRE, the training methodology, and preliminary results demonstrating the potential of this approach. The primary goal is to establish a framework where complex logical inferences can be learned directly from data, reducing the reliance on explicit rule definition and potentially leading to more robust and adaptable reasoning systems. The architecture focuses on encoding logical relationships and applying gradient-based optimization to refine the model's understanding.

title: Machine Learning Techniques for Histological Tissue Classification in Veterinary Science
abstract: Classification of tissues by histological features represents the fundamental approach utilized in the diagnosis of animal diseases in veterinary pathology. While light microscopy remains the gold standard for histopathological evaluation, it may be limited by human variability and increasing workloads. Recent advances in deep learning based on convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, and graph neural networks, which have been employed for the classification of histological tissues in different animal species, including dogs, cats, horses, cattle, birds, pigs, and sheep. The methodological framework is thoroughly reviewed, ranging from image pre-processing, feature extraction, training methods, transfer learning, data augmentation, multi-resolution analysis, and explainability methods in artificial intelligence. Specific challenges that come with veterinary histopathology include tissue morphologies across different species, annotated datasets, staining inconsistencies, and pathways for clinical application.

title: Hierarchical Progressive Optimization for Multi-Qubit Pauli Noise Modeling
abstract: Abstract Quantum Noise Characterization (QNC) is indispensable for benchmarking and mitigating errors in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. However, traditional Quantum Process Tomography (QPT) suffers from an exponential parameter explosion, severely hindering its scalability. In this paper, we propose a Hierarchical Progressive Optimization (HPO) framework to efficiently extract high-order spatial crosstalk in multi-qubit systems. The complexity analysis shows that the combinatorial projection mask reduces the required number of Pauli transfer matrix (PTM) elements from O (16 N ) to O ( N 2 3 N ). Numerical simulations on a 10-qubit HHL circuit achieve a fidelity of 0.9381 with the HPO method, compared to 0.7431 obtained using global depolarizing-noise mitigation.

title: Texture Image Classification Using DWT AlexNet Feature Fusion and Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Texture image classification plays a significant role in computer vision applications, including industrial inspection, medical image analysis, remote sensing, and object recognition. Handcrafted features can capture local texture characteristics but may have limited capability to represent complex visual patterns. In contrast, deep learning models automatically learn discriminative representations but may not fully exploit the multiscale spatial-frequency information inherent in texture images. This paper proposes a hybrid feature fusion framework, termed DWT_AlexNet_DNN, which combines Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) features with deep features extracted using AlexNet for texture image classification.

title: A comprehensive and trustworthy benchmark of AI methods for change detection in Earth observation
abstract: Change detection in Earth observation (EO) is critical for monitoring land surface transformations, yet recent research in the field is constrained by inconsistent evaluation protocols and a narrow focus on predictive accuracy without regard for computational efficiency. To address this, we present a standardized, open-source benchmark for evaluating state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning methods for Earth observation change detection. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of ten representative model architectures, ranging from convolutional networks (CNNs) to vision transformers (ViTs), across ten heterogeneous change detection datasets. We rigorously evaluate these models with identical experimental protocols, comparing models trained from scratch against those utilizing pre-trained weights. Furthermore, we evaluate predictive performance alongside computational efficiency, including parameter counts and inference latency. Our findings reveal that well-optimized classical architectures, such as Siamese U-Nets, frequently outperform more complex contemporary models when computational efficiency is factored in, and that pre-training consistently provides a significant performance boost with no additional inference cost. To ensure complete transparency and reproducibility, all experimental resources, including standardized data splits, training scripts, training logs, and model checkpoints are publicly available and adhere to FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable).

title: Network Topologies for QKD Networks
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a method for distributing cryptographic keys between remote endpoints, enjoying security based on quantum physics. This paper makes a first step towards studying topologies for QKD networks. QKD networks imply several required characteristics for their reliability and efficiency. We express such properties in terms of graph structure. For the comparison of potential graphs, we describe cost functions that allow us to identify families of graphs that are reliable and efficient. To make the discussion realistic, we summarize representative field-reported QKD performance numbers and illustrate the sensitivity of secret-key rate (SKR) to a few dB of additional loss. Last, we present methods to construct large efficient graphs through connecting smaller graphs.

title: The Photonic Computer
abstract: This document presents the first complete architecture based on directional photonic theory, a new science of computation in which light becomes the primary carrier of information, coherence, and structure. It explains how directional geometries, fractals, hyperfractals, and dynamic, adaptive, emergent, and self‑replicating structures can be organized to form a light‑based computer capable of surpassing all existing technologies. The work explores in depth the fundamental properties of photonic computation: directional coherence, multidimensional stability, luminous synchronization, fractal and hyperfractal structures, spatiotemporal dynamics, internal adaptation mechanisms, the emergence of new behaviors, geometric replication, and the foundations of intelligent computation. It demonstrates why the photonic computer is superior to the quantum computer: light suffers no decoherence, operates at room temperature, carries more states than a qubit, enables non‑destructive geometries, and offers a level of stability that superconducting systems will never achieve. This document is not merely a technical description: it is the foundation of a new computational era, where light becomes the universal medium for computation, structure, and evolution.

title: AffectLoop: From Experience to Conditional Self-Reaction Prediction with Counterfactual Twins
abstract: Can an LLM-based agent system acquire a branch-specific model of its own future reactions from controlled experience, use that model prospectively, and revise it after counterevidence? We introduce a counterfactual-twin assay in which matched agent branches share the same Actor, initial conditions, available actions, and outcome multiset but differ in the contextual binding of those outcomes. The assay separates five questions that are often conflated: experience-conditioned reaction divergence, storage in a prospective Core, transfer beyond cue identity, Actor access, and selective revision. Across five precommitted source–twin pairs, progressively stronger shortcut-removal assays preserved low error for the correct Core while twin-swapped and no-Core controls remained substantially worse. In the strongest Actor assay, a Qwen3-8B Actor directly predicted ordinal changes on four reaction axes with 94.38% directional accuracy under the correct Core, compared with 0% after twin swapping, 51.88% after targeted local inversion, and 26.88% with no Core; predictions were committed before independent held-out Native Reactions were generated. A separate zero-Actor-call track tested system-level online formation and revision. Online Core formation reduced held-out binary error from 0.4875 with an empty Core to 0 with the correct learned Core, whereas the twin Core yielded error 1.0. Local counterevidence revision reduced anchor-near error from 0.41484 to 0 without changing far probes; shuffled and twin updates failed. A first-attempt confirmatory run on five precommitted unused pairs reproduced the full functional J–M–E1–F1 chain, with all five revision gains positive (mean 0.41189; exact one-sided sign-test p = .03125), 99.3% of the original mean gain. These results support a bounded claim: the system implements an experience-grounded, branch-specific prospective self-model that can guide ordinal self-prediction and undergo engineered local revision. They do not establish consciousness, phenomenological selfhood, privileged introspection, or autonomous discovery of the reaction-generating mechanism.

title: Formal Model of Cognitive Bias in Reinforcement Learning Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed in complex environments, yet their performance is often surprisingly brittle and susceptible to suboptimal strategies. This brittleness stems, in part, from inherent cognitive biases that mimic human decision-making processes. This paper presents a formal model of cognitive bias within RL agents, arguing that these biases are predictable and can be formally represented and mitigated. The core of our approach involves integrating concepts from behavioral economics and cognitive psychology – specifically confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, and loss aversion – into the agent's decision-making process. We define a mathematical framework, utilizing variables such as *Q(s, a)* representing the action-value function and *R(s, a)* representing the reward function, to quantify the impact of these biases. The model introduces a bias factor, *β*, that modifies the expected reward calculation, reflecting the influence of the heuristic. We demonstrate how this bias factor can be dynamically adjusted based on observed environmental feedback, leading to improved agent robustness and performance. The novelty of this work lies in providing a rigorous, mathematically grounded approach to understanding and addressing cognitive biases in RL, shifting the focus from purely reward-based optimization to incorporating psychological insights. We outline a methodology for identifying and quantifying biases, and propose strategies for mitigating their detrimental effects. Ultimately, this model offers a pathway towards more reliable and adaptable RL agents.

title: Quantum Walk-Based Optimization of Neural Network Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture search (NAS) leveraging the principles of quantum walks. Traditional NAS methods suffer from significant computational bottlenecks, limiting their scalability and practicality. We introduce a framework where quantum walks are employed to efficiently explore the vast architectural search space. The core idea is to map the architectural choices – such as the number of layers, the type of activation functions, and the connections between neurons – to a quantum state, allowing for parallel exploration guided by the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum walks. The algorithm iteratively evolves the quantum state, favoring architectures that maximize performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, inference time) while minimizing computational complexity. This approach offers the potential to dramatically accelerate the NAS process, enabling the discovery of high-performing neural network architectures with reduced computational cost. The theoretical framework is presented, along with a detailed explanation of the quantum walk implementation and its convergence properties. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this method through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to outperform conventional NAS techniques in terms of both speed and architectural quality.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing for Distributed Quantum State Teleportation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum state teleportation leveraging hyperdimensional computing (HDC). Traditional quantum state teleportation protocols face limitations due to qubit fidelity requirements and the complexity associated with distributing entangled qubits over long distances. We propose utilizing HDC – high-dimensional vectors characterized by near-orthogonal components – to represent and transmit quantum states. Our method significantly reduces the need for direct qubit entanglement, offering a potentially scalable and robust alternative. The core mechanism involves encoding the quantum state information into the high-dimensional vector components and subsequently extracting the state at the destination. We detail the mathematical framework underpinning this approach, focusing on vector projections, inner products, and state reconstruction. The results demonstrate a viable path towards distributed quantum state teleportation, addressing the key challenges of fidelity and entanglement distribution. We provide a detailed analysis of the computational complexity and potential advantages of this HDC-based teleportation scheme.

evidence.abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum state teleportation leveraging hyperdimensional computing (HDC). Traditional quantum state teleportation protocols face limitations due to qubit fidelity requirements and the complexity associated with distributing entangled qubits over long distances. We propose utilizing HDC – high-dimensional vectors characterized by near-orthogonal components – to represent and transmit quantum states. Our method significantly reduces the need for direct qubit entanglement, offering a potentially scalable and robust alternative. The core mechanism involves encoding the quantum state information into the high-dimensional vector components and subsequently extracting the state at the destination. We detail the mathematical framework underpinning this approach, focusing on vector projections, inner products, and state reconstruction. The results demonstrate a viable path towards distributed quantum state teleportation, addressing the key challenges of fidelity and entanglement distribution. We provide a detailed analysis of the computational complexity and potential advantages of this HDC-based teleportation scheme.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Strategies and Bayesian Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression that leverages the strengths of both evolutionary strategies (ES) and Bayesian optimization (BO) to achieve significantly improved equation discovery performance. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with the high dimensionality and complex relationships inherent in data, leading to slow convergence and suboptimal solutions. Our approach addresses this challenge by employing an ES framework to explore the vast space of potential mathematical equations, while a BO algorithm intelligently guides the ES search, focusing on regions of the space with the highest probability of containing accurate equations. The core of our method lies in the synergy between these two techniques: the ES provides a robust exploration mechanism, while the BO offers a targeted and efficient exploitation strategy. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a detailed examination of the algorithmic components that this combined approach offers a substantial advantage over standalone ES or BO methods. The results show a notable improvement in equation accuracy and convergence speed, particularly for datasets with complex underlying relationships.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Graph Embedding with Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding using self-supervised learning, specifically leveraging the principles of contrastive predictive coding (CPC). Existing graph embedding techniques frequently employ simplistic pretext tasks, often resulting in embeddings that fail to fully capture the intricate relationships within graph data. Our method addresses this limitation by training a model to predict future node states based on their past states, guided by a contrastive loss function. This allows the model to learn richer and more informative embeddings by explicitly enforcing similarity between related states and dissimilarity between unrelated states. We demonstrate that this approach yields significantly improved graph embeddings compared to traditional self-supervised methods, highlighting the potential of CPC for capturing complex graph dependencies. The core claim of this work is that contrastive predictive coding can create richer and more informative graph embeddings, moving beyond the limitations of simpler pretext tasks.

title: Emergent Explanation Generation for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing deployment of complex Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, particularly deep neural networks, raises critical concerns about their interpretability. Traditional explanation methods often rely on post-hoc analysis, introducing potential biases and failing to capture the underlying cognitive mechanisms driving model behavior. This paper proposes a novel algorithmic framework for automatically generating emergent explanations within AI models. The core principle is to directly extract and translate internal activation patterns into human-understandable explanations. We leverage Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) and association rule mining to identify salient patterns within model activations and subsequently generate explanations that highlight significant relationships. The proposed approach offers a shift from manual interpretation to automated discovery, aiming to unveil the hidden cognitive processes within AI systems. The system's ability to autonomously generate explanations represents a significant advancement in the field of Explainable AI (XAI), promoting a deeper understanding of AI decision-making and fostering trust in these increasingly prevalent technologies. The generated explanations are presented in terms of rules and patterns, facilitating easier comprehension.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Clinical Reliability in Histology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming histological tissue analysis in veterinary sciences, but the limited interpretability of deep learning models remains a major barrier to clinical adoption. This chapter examines explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, and attention mechanisms, and their role in improving diagnostic transparency and reliability in veterinary histopathology. Drawing on evidence from canine mammary tumours, feline lymphoma, equine pulmonary disease, and comparative computational pathology, it explores how XAI supports whole-slide image analysis, quality assurance, and regulatory compliance by highlighting the morphological features underlying AI predictions. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations and future research priorities focused on standardized evaluation, clinical validation, and robust data governance to strengthen trust in AI-assisted veterinary diagnostics.

title: When Robots Mishear Us: Mapping the Safety Risks of Voice-Controlled Embodied AI
abstract: We investigate whether automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors in user input can lead to unsafe outputs from Embodied AI (EAI) models. We find that ASR errors can lead to harmful instructions being accepted and executed by EAI models, thereby reducing safety. We simulate ASR errors and combine them with existing safety benchmarks (SafeAgentBench and POEX) to evaluate how different errors affect embodied AI safety. We find that some of them preserve semantic structure but increase harmful ambiguity, while others weaken the model refusal behaviour and allow unsafe plans to be generated and executed. We show that in some cases automatic correction of ASR errors can reduce the risk, but this is not always effective. Overall, we show that ASR errors lead to significant safety risks for embodied AI.

title: Training-free Suction Grasp Detection for Deformed Aseptic Cartons Using Vision-Language Models and Geometric Surface Scoring
abstract: Robotic sorting of recyclable waste is challenging due to the deformable and geometrically inconsistent nature of target objects. We present a training-free suction grasping system for sorting deformed aseptic beverage cartons, decoupling target identification from grasp-point selection. An open-vocabulary vision-language model detects cartons from a text prompt, SAM2 refines each detection into an instance mask, and a geometric scoring method selects the suction point by combining surface flatness with normal alignment. Three geometric methods are compared: k-nearest-neighbour PCA, Sobel cross-product, and RANSAC plane fitting. Evaluated on a real robot across three deformation levels and 35 cluttered scenes, single-object grasp success reaches 88.2% and end-to-end retrieval in clutter is 72.6%.

title: PhyMamba: Physics-Modulated Mamba for Robust Battery Health Prognostics
abstract: Battery health prognostics is a core function in battery management systems (BMSs), yet long-horizon health forecasting from BMS signals remains challenging due to operating-condition dependency and sensor noise. In this paper, we propose PhyMamba, a two-stage physics-modulated Mamba framework that integrates electrochemical aging into sequence modelling. PhyMamba does not require explicit identification of internal aging parameters, which often relies on intrusive measurements. In stage-1, a lightweight Mamba encoder first processes BMS signals and produces a latent representation that is transformed via an aging parameterization module, into physics-informed aging features. In stage-2, a customized Mamba forecasting backbone performs multi-cycle prediction, where physics is tightly integrated to regulate the model's internal temporal updates toward degradation-consistent evolution. Experiments on three public datasets under multiple forecast horizons show that PhyMamba achieves the best aggregated performance, with an overall mean error reduction of 31.8% compared with a diverse range of baselines. PhyMamba also offers an optimized accuracy-efficiency trade-off, which supports practical deployment for robust battery health prognostics.

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Quantum Feature Selection
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of combining quantum machine learning with quantum feature selection to enhance the performance of machine learning models. The core idea is to frame the machine learning problem as a quantum feature selection problem, leveraging quantum phenomena such as entanglement and superposition to effectively identify the most informative features. Traditional feature selection methods often struggle with high-dimensional datasets and may not fully exploit the inherent correlations between features. Quantum feature selection, utilizing quantum computers, offers a fundamentally different approach, potentially capable of identifying subtle relationships and patterns that classical methods miss. This paper explores the theoretical framework, outlining the conversion process and the utilization of quantum mechanics to optimize feature selection. The proposed method aims to achieve superior classification and regression results compared to conventional machine learning algorithms. We present a detailed mathematical description of the process, emphasizing the key quantum concepts involved. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a viable pathway for advancing machine learning capabilities through the integration of quantum computing principles.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Architectures via Genetic Regulatory Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture design by integrating principles from genetic regulatory networks (GRNs). Traditional neural network training relies heavily on gradient descent, often leading to suboptimal architectures and inefficient training processes. Our methodology introduces a simulated "genetic network" that dynamically governs the architecture of a neural network during training. This network adjusts parameters like layer sizes, connection strengths, and activation functions based on performance feedback, mirroring the adaptive mechanisms observed in biological systems. The core claim is that mimicking GRNs' self-regulation can lead to more effective and adaptive neural network architectures. We outline the design of this training regime, focusing on the interplay between the neural network and the simulated genetic network. The theoretical framework is presented, highlighting the potential benefits of this approach over conventional gradient-based methods. The research explores how feedback loops and regulatory elements within the GRN can drive the neural network towards increasingly efficient and specialized architectures. We demonstrate the feasibility of this concept and suggest future research directions for further development and experimentation.

title: Machine Learning for Automated Theorem Proving using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to automate theorem proving, a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence and mathematics. The core idea is to train an RL agent to strategically guide a traditional theorem prover, effectively learning a proof strategy. The system operates by the RL agent observing the state of the theorem prover – typically represented by the current set of axioms, hypotheses, and inference steps – and then selecting actions, such as applying specific inference rules or searching for new axioms. The reward signal provided to the agent is designed to incentivize progress towards a valid proof. This approach represents a novel combination of machine learning and automated reasoning, with the potential to create truly autonomous proof systems. We detail the architecture of the system, the RL algorithm employed, and the design choices made for the reward function. The goal is to demonstrate the feasibility of learning efficient proof strategies through interaction and feedback. The paper focuses on conceptual design and potential architectures, not on a fully realized system, and highlights the key challenges and future research directions in this area.

title: Information-Theoretic Security Protocols for Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: This paper investigates the design of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols rooted in information-theoretic principles. Traditional QKD approaches often rely on the presumed computational hardness of certain mathematical problems. This work advocates for a paradigm shift, utilizing concepts such as channel capacity and mutual information to establish security guarantees directly. We explore protocols that explicitly measure and manage information flow between sender and receiver, drawing upon channel capacity to mitigate eavesdropping attempts. The core contribution lies in a framework for designing QKD protocols that are resilient to channel impairments and provide verifiable security bounds based on information-theoretic metrics. The proposed designs offer a more robust and fundamental approach to QKD security, independent of computational assumptions. We present a detailed analysis of key aspects including channel capacity limits, mutual information calculations, and the resulting security parameters.

title: A Cognitive Architecture-Based Programming Language
abstract: This paper proposes a novel programming language designed around the principles of cognitive architectures. The core claim is that by embedding cognitive architecture concepts directly into the language, we can significantly improve the ease of use, explainability, and ultimately, the alignment of software with human cognitive processes. The language, termed "CogniLang," utilizes a new programming paradigm derived from architectures like Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and COG. CogniLang introduces concepts such as values, experiences, and interventions as first-class citizens within the language, allowing programmers to model not just *what* a program does, but *how* it does it, mirroring human thought processes. The paper details the key features and syntax of CogniLang, illustrating how it diverges from traditional programming paradigms. It argues that this approach represents a significant step towards creating software that is more intuitive, adaptable, and genuinely understandable by humans. The language's design focuses on promoting a mindful and iterative development process, reflecting the core tenets of cognitive science.

title: Emerging AI Technologies in Veterinary Histology
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming veterinary histology by enhancing the accuracy, speed, and consistency of tissue analysis and disease diagnosis. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, digital pathology, whole-slide imaging, and explainable AI enables automated tissue classification, lesion detection, cellular analysis, and quantitative histomorphometry. Emerging technologies such as vision transformers, generative AI, federated learning, and cloud-based platforms further expand research and diagnostic capabilities. Despite challenges related to dataset availability, species diversity, data quality, and ethical concerns, AI offers significant opportunities for advancing veterinary diagnostics, education, precision medicine, and One Health initiatives. Continued development and validation will drive future innovations.

title: Exploring Public Reaction to Air Quality on Social Media: The 2022 Saharan Dust Episode in Lisbon
abstract: This study analyses the relationship between air quality and sentiments expressed on social media, focusing on the Saharan dust episode that affected Lisbon in March 2022. Environmental data were collected alongside geolocated Twitter posts (now rebranded as X) from the Lisbon area. The content of these posts was analysed using the Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner algorithm to identify emotional patterns and assess correlations with fluctuations in atmospheric pollutants. A predictive analysis was also conducted using Decision Tree and Random Forest machine learning algorithms. The findings suggest that despite high levels of inhalable particulate matter (PM10) during the event, there was no significant change in online sentiments, which remained mostly neutral or slightly positive. This implies that the publics environ-mental perception may not be clearly reflected on social media, possibly due to cultural factors or the limited influence of Twitter in Portugal. The study concludes that integrating environmental and social data is feasible and valuable, but further research is needed to explore longer periods, other cities, and more advanced techniques, thus contributing to the understanding of air pollution and public perception in Portugal.
