title: DisCTI: Who Needs to Know Timely? Automated Sector-Aware Cyber Threat Intelligence Dissemination
abstract: The timely dissemination of cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is critical for organizations to mount swift and effective incident response. When valid CTI is delivered to the right sector at the right time, identical attacks can often be contained or mitigated. However, today's rapidly expanding CTI landscape overwhelms analysts, who must sift through massive and heterogeneous feeds. Existing platforms such as the Malware Information Sharing Platform (MISP) provide sector tagging features (e.g., energy, finance, government), but in practice, these remain largely unmapped (98% of events are left uncategorized). This lack of automated and timely sector mapping severely limits the operational value of shared intelligence, leaving organizations that belong especially to the critical information infrastructure sector exposed. To address this gap, we formulate sector-targeted CTI dissemination as a multilabel classification problem. Leveraging deep field knowledge of CTI structures and sector-specific threat patterns, we construct a novel data set of 872 sector-labelled CTI events from a threat intelligence platform (TIP). evidence.title: DisCTI: Who Needs to Know Timely? Automated Sector-Aware Cyber Threat Intelligence Dissemination
evidence.abstract: The timely dissemination of cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is critical for organizations to mount swift and effective incident response. When valid CTI is delivered to the right sector at the right time, identical attacks can often be contained or mitigated. However, today's rapidly expanding CTI landscape overwhelms analysts, who must sift through massive and heterogeneous feeds. Existing platforms such as the Malware Information Sharing Platform (MISP) provide sector tagging features (e.g., energy, finance, government), but in practice, these remain largely unmapped (98% of events are left uncategorized). This lack of automated and timely sector mapping severely limits the operational value of shared intelligence, leaving organizations that belong especially to the critical information infrastructure sector exposed. To address this gap, we formulate sector-targeted CTI dissemination as a multilabel classification problem. Leveraging deep field knowledge of CTI structures and sector-specific threat patterns, we construct a novel data set of 872 sector-labelled CTI events from a threat intelligence platform (TIP). We then apply BERT, a transformer-based model, to automate the mapping of CTI events to sectors. Using the structured threat information expression (STIX) format for cross-platform interoperability, our approach achieves a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.89 at a Hamming loss of 0.055 on the custom dataset, i.e. 94.5% of individual sector-label assignments are correct. title: XAIoT: a Conceptual Model for XAI Solutions on IoT
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are part of our current world, helping us to perform a wide variety of tasks. In parallel, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which obtains explanations to help users understand AI systems, has increased in significance in the last few years. This relevance comes from users’ necessity to trust new complex AI models. However, AI is not confined to computers but is also applied to other devices to use current internet connectivity to make our lives easier. The already well-known Internet of Things (IoT) refers to this digitally connected universe of smart devices. Hence, XAI should also be applied to the IoT, although there is a gap in the literature concerning conceptualizing explanation methods applied to AI models on the IoT. In this work, we propose a conceptual model named XAIoT (eXplainable Artificial Intelligence of Things) that structures and formalizes the main features of such systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a framework that guides the selection of the most suitable XAI solution for a given intelligent IoT application. This conceptual model is validated by classifying up to 100 approaches obtained from a systematic review of the state-of-the-art and formalized in an ontology to guide XAIoT system design.

title: Why Enterprise AI Pilots Fail: From PoC to Production
abstract: We built an AI anomaly detector that worked perfectly—until 89% of users disabled it on first login. The problem wasn't accuracy. It was inserting sophisticated prediction into a workflow that never needed it. Here's why most enterprise AI pilots never escape the PoC phase. title: Learning-Native Adaptive Software Framework (LNASF): Research Positioning and Candidate Component Contract
abstract: A research working draft for the Learning-Native Adaptive Software Framework (LNASF). It proposes a candidate component-boundary contract that makes observation, model updating, prediction evidence, adaptation admission, permitted actions, deterministic fallback, and outcome evaluation explicit. The candidate contribution is under validation against prior work on online runtime learning, ML-enabled components, self-adaptive architectures, FORMS, Rainbow, adaptive feedback loops, and prior usage of the learning-native software concept. Novelty and performance benefits are not yet established. The repository includes the research draft, preliminary prior-art comparison, and compiled PDF. This is not a peer-reviewed paper.

title: Scaling Effects on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in XTREME Benchmark Performance
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does scaling the size of the language model affect the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on the XTREME benchmark when trained with English intermediate tasks, as measured by accuracy and F1 score? title: #基于多模态信息融合的预测性异常检测
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to predictive anomaly detection by fusing multiple modalities of information. The core idea is to leverage prior knowledge embedded within diverse data sources – including images, text, and time series – to enhance the accuracy and timeliness of anomaly detection, particularly in complex systems. We propose a framework utilizing Transformer architectures for multimodal information integration, coupled with causal models for predicting system behavior. The system continuously monitors and alerts on potential anomalies based on a defined anomaly metric. Unlike traditional methods limited to single-modality detection, our approach addresses the inherent limitations by combining information from multiple sources, significantly improving detection accuracy and reducing false alarms. The framework offers a robust solution for predictive anomaly detection in scenarios where anomalies are often subtle and difficult to identify using isolated data streams. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline key considerations for its implementation. ---

title: Dynamically Adaptive Neural Network Architectures via Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of evolutionary algorithms to dynamically design and optimize neural network architectures. Traditional neural network design relies heavily on human expertise, often involving extensive trial and error. This manual process can be time-consuming and may not always yield the most effective architectures for a given task. We propose a framework where an evolutionary algorithm autonomously modifies a neural network's structure based on its performance feedback. The algorithm iteratively evolves the architecture – adjusting parameters such as layer count, connectivity, and activation functions – driven by a fitness function that correlates with task performance. The core claim is that evolutionary algorithms can effectively automate this design process, leading to the discovery of optimal network structures without the need for extensive human intervention. This approach offers the potential to significantly reduce the design time and improve the performance of neural networks across a wide range of applications. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this method through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and considerations for implementation.

title: Anomaly Detection Based on Multivariate Normal Distribution
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to anomaly detection leveraging the statistical properties of multivariate normal distributions. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and complex dependencies. By representing data as multivariate normal distributions and analyzing their deviations from expected behavior, we can effectively identify anomalous patterns. This method offers a computationally efficient and interpretable solution for various applications, including network intrusion detection, equipment fault diagnosis, and process monitoring. The core idea involves dimensionality reduction and feature extraction, transforming the data into a multivariate normal distribution. We then utilize statistical tests based on the distribution's parameters and residuals to flag deviations indicative of anomalies. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, providing a foundation for further research and practical implementation. We present a framework that emphasizes the use of principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction and robust statistical tests for anomaly scoring.

title: A Hybrid AES–NTRU Cryptographic Framework with Deterministic Dynamic S-Box for Secure Data Transmission
abstract: The rapid expansion of interconnected sensing and monitoring systems has significantly increased the volume of digital data exchanged across distributed environments. While these systems provide substantial benefits for real-time monitoring and automated decision making, they also introduce critical challenges related to data confidentiality and secure communication. This study proposes a hybrid cryptographic framework designed to strengthen secure data transmission in distributed sensing environments. The primary objective of this research is to integrate a symmetric encryption mechanism with a lattice-based public-key cryptographic scheme within a hybrid key protection architecture. In addition, a deterministic round-dependent substitution mechanism is introduced into the symmetric encryption process to provide controlled structural variability during data encryption while preserving compatibility with the standard round-based encryption structure. The proposed framework was implemented in a software-based prototype environment and evaluated through a series of encryption and decryption experiments using representative data payloads that emulate typical communication scenarios in distributed sensing systems. The evaluation focused on three aspects: implementation correctness, computational performance, and diffusion characteristics of the encryption process. Experimental results confirm that all encrypted data payloads were successfully decrypted to their original plaintext without bit errors, demonstrating the functional correctness of the integrated cryptographic architecture. The encryption process achieved an avalanche effect of 47.01 percent, with an average encryption time of 118.99 milliseconds and a decryption time of 5.91 milliseconds in the prototype environment. These results indicate consistent diffusion behavior within acceptable experimental bounds while maintaining reasonable computational overhead for gateway-level communication nodes. The findings suggest that integrating adaptive substitution mechanisms within hybrid cryptographic architectures can provide flexible encryption structures suitable for secure data transmission in distributed monitoring systems, while remaining compatible with widely deployed symmetric encryption frameworks.

title: Emerging Advances in Tissue Classification Using AI in Veterinary Histopathology
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming veterinary histopathology by enabling rapid, accurate, and automated tissue classification. The integration of digital pathology, machine learning, deep learning, and whole-slide imaging has enhanced the detection of normal and diseased tissues, tumors, inflammatory lesions, and infectious diseases across diverse animal species. Advanced models such as Convolutional Neural Networks, Vision Transformers, and hybrid learning frameworks improve diagnostic precision while reducing observer variability and workload. AI-assisted image analysis, segmentation, biomarker identification, and decision-support systems contribute to precision veterinary medicine. Despite challenges related to data availability, standardization, and ethics, AI offers significant potential for future veterinary diagnostics.

title: D-TAIA: Domain-Aware LLM Adaptation for Multi-Task Predictive Process Monitoring
abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) enables organizations to forecast future process behavior, such as the next activity and remaining time of ongoing cases. In practice, three conditions cause existing methods to degrade, namely data scarcity, high process entropy and distributional shift. While Foundation Models (FMs), especially Large Language Models (LLMs), offer a new paradigm through broad sequential reasoning, adapting them to multi-task PPM under these conditions remains an open challenge. Existing FM-based approaches either lack mechanisms for handling distributional shift or rely on direct regression heads that can be structurally misaligned with continuous time prediction tasks. This paper introduces D-TAIA (Domain-aware Training and Attention-based Inference Architecture), a framework for a joint next activity and remaining time prediction task via parameter-efficient fine-tuning of an FM backbone. Our approach combines domain-aware triplet loss (DATL) pre-training with FAISS-based nearest neighbor retrieval for remaining time prediction, and adopts the TAIA inference strategy to preserve pre-trained sequential reasoning during fine-tuning. Evaluated across four real-world event logs, D-TAIA consistently shows SOTA or competitive performance compared to a fine-tuned LLM and a recurrent neural network baseline. Ablation studies confirm that techniques from NLP and computer vision can be transferred effectively to PPM with only a 10M-parameter backbone, though component contributions vary by dataset entropy.

title: Lexically conditioned realization ambiguity in Korean predicate morphology
abstract: This paper examines Korean surface realization as distinct from morphological analysis. It asks whether a sequence of canonical morphemes and grammatical category labels uniquely determines the corresponding surface form. The answer is negative for a restricted but theoretically revealing class of Korean predicates. In these cases, formally identical or near-identical stem-ending configurations yield different outputs depending on lexical identity and realization class membership. We analyze this phenomenon as homonymy with inflectional divergence, focusing on regular versus digeut irregular pairs, regular versus bieup irregular pairs, and reu irregular versus reo irregular pairs. These cases show that stem shape and ending alone do not always determine surface realization. Instead, lexical meaning, subcategorization, and semantic role structure help identify the intended predicate; the predicate determines the realization class; and the realization class determines the surface form. Korean realization thus reveals a limit of bare morphological representation.

title: Is Your VPN Getting You Blocked?
abstract: There are many valid reasons for someone to browse the internet privately, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) are one method of achieving this. Although primarily used to provide confidentiality and anonymity by encrypting internet traffic and masking IP addresses, users may choose to use a VPN for multiple purposes. However, this raises questions about whether, and how differently, content across the internet is portrayed to VPN users. VPN providers do not all route their traffic the same way, and this study analyzes these differences by investigating two major VPN providers, NordVPN and Surfshark. We measure and quantify the accessibility of popular websites to users of these two VPNs, comparing outcomes against a non-VPN control connection to determine whether, and to what extent, VPN use affects a user's ability to reach and use ordinary websites. This raises a central question: is VPN-related blocking better explained by the network a VPN happens to use, or by where its exit server is physically located? To investigate this, requests to the Tranco top 10,000 domains were compared between each VPN and a non-VPN control connection to measure blocking at full scale. A second set of experiments isolated exit servers by network (ASN) and by physical location across a smaller domain set, allowing the effects of these factors to be compared. At full scale, NordVPN showed 1.59\% VPN-attributable blocking and Surfshark showed 0.42\%. When exit servers were isolated by ASN and location, block-rate variation did not show a clear difference between the two factors, while the network path taken by a request varied substantially with location. These results suggest that VPN-related blocking is not explained by a single infrastructural factor, but instead depends on multiple properties of the network through which a VPN request is routed, including characteristics of the individual exit, network infrastructure, and geographic location. At full scale, NordVPN showed 1.59\% VPN-attributable blocking and Surfshark showed 0.42\%, measured across the Tranco top 10,000 domains using a single exit per provider. Under infrastructure isolation across five ASNs and five countries, crawling top 200 domains, block-rate variation was similar whether ASN or location was held fixed (2.5\% vs. 4.0\% mean within-group range). Per-provider significance testing further found that only a small number of ASNs showed significant differences in blocking. In contrast, network routing varied substantially with exit location: CDN routing varied by 76\% when location was held fixed, compared with 58\% when ASN was held fixed. These results suggest that VPN-related blocking is not explained by a single infrastructural factor, but instead depends on multiple properties of the specific exit and network path through which a VPN request is routed.

evidence.title: Is Your VPN Getting You Blocked?
evidence.abstract: There are many valid reasons for someone to browse the internet privately, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) are one method of achieving this. Although primarily used to provide confidentiality and anonymity by encrypting internet traffic and masking IP addresses, users may choose to use a VPN for multiple purposes. However, this raises questions about whether, and how differently, content across the internet is portrayed to VPN users. VPN providers do not all route their traffic the same way, and this study analyzes these differences by investigating two major VPN providers, NordVPN and Surfshark. We measure and quantify the accessibility of popular websites to users of these two VPNs, comparing outcomes against a non-VPN control connection to determine whether, and to what extent, VPN use affects a user's ability to reach and use ordinary websites. This raises a central question: is VPN-related blocking better explained by the network a VPN happens to use, or by where its exit server is physically located? To investigate this, requests to the Tranco top 10,000 domains were compared between each VPN and a non-VPN control connection to measure blocking at full scale. A second set of experiments isolated exit servers by network (ASN) and by physical location across a smaller domain set, allowing the effects of these factors to be compared. At full scale, NordVPN showed 1.59\% VPN-attributable blocking and Surfshark showed 0.42\%. When exit servers were isolated by ASN and location, block-rate variation did not show a clear difference between the two factors, while the network path taken by a request varied substantially with location. These results suggest that VPN-related blocking is not explained by a single infrastructural factor, but instead depends on multiple properties of the network through which a VPN request is routed, including characteristics of the individual exit, network infrastructure, and geographic location. At full scale, NordVPN showed 1.59\% VPN-attributable blocking and Surfshark showed 0.42\%, measured across the Tranco top 10,000 domains using a single exit per provider. Under infrastructure isolation across five ASNs and five countries, crawling top 200 domains, block-rate variation was similar whether ASN or location was held fixed (2.5\% vs. 4.0\% mean within-group range). Per-provider significance testing further found that only a small number of ASNs showed significant differences in blocking. In contrast, network routing varied substantially with exit location: CDN routing varied by 76\% when location was held fixed, compared with 58\% when ASN was held fixed. These results suggest that VPN-related blocking is not explained by a single infrastructural factor, but instead depends on multiple properties of the specific exit and network path through which a VPN request is routed.

title: Spectral Graph Clustering with Dynamic Spectrum Allocation
abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of traditional spectral clustering methods when applied to dynamic graphs, where the underlying connectivity changes over time. Traditional spectral clustering relies on a fixed spectrum derived from the graph Laplacian, which can be significantly affected by noise and may not adapt to evolving graph structures. We propose a novel framework for spectral graph clustering that incorporates dynamic spectrum allocation. This mechanism adjusts the weighting of different graph components based on their current relevance, effectively optimizing the clustering process for the specific graph state. The core idea is to continuously update the spectrum, reflecting the changing connectivity patterns. We formalize this approach with mathematical equations, detailing the dynamic Laplacian construction and the associated clustering algorithm. This dynamic approach improves robustness to noise and offers a more accurate solution for clustering in environments where the graph structure is inherently unstable. The proposed method is evaluated conceptually, providing a foundation for future experimental validation and extension.

title: KAIRÆLUM v0.2 — Public Research Release
abstract: KAIRÆLUM v0.2 Overview KAIRÆLUM v0.2 is a discrete-time recurrent state architecture built around a primary state vector, fast and slow memory states, and an adaptive internal threshold. The architecture is developed as an experimental framework for studying recurrent state evolution, memory timescales, adaptive gating, persistence, and local dynamical stability. Public Research Release This public research release freezes the KAIRÆLUM v0.2 architecture together with its canonical implementation, five analysis and benchmark scripts, machine-readable result artifacts, and the final whitepaper. Epistemic Scope The release maintains a strict distinction between: implemented mechanisms; empirically measured behavior; analytical local stability results; proposed theoretical and geometric extensions that are not implemented in the v0.2 core. The accompanying whitepaper is the authoritative description of the architecture, benchmark protocols, numerical results, analytical scope, limitations, and proposed geometric program. Claims and Limitations KAIRÆLUM v0.2 does not claim to establish: long-term semantic memory; prevention of catastrophic forgetting; global nonlinear stability; biological equivalence; artificial consciousness. These boundaries define the evidential scope of the v0.2 release and do not extend beyond the results documented in the accompanying whitepaper and benchmark artifacts.

title: Non-Classical Correlation Entropy as a Measure of Quantum State Measurement Trustworthiness
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for assessing the trustworthiness of quantum state measurement results based on non-classical correlation entropy. The core idea revolves around quantifying the correlation within quantum states using this entropy measure. By analyzing the associated entropy, we can evaluate the reliability of measurement outcomes and subsequently propose corrective and optimization strategies. Traditional approaches to quantum measurement uncertainty often rely on probabilistic interpretations and lack a direct quantification of the inherent correlations within the quantum state itself. This work aims to bridge this gap by providing a framework for assessing trustworthiness rooted in the fundamental properties of quantum entanglement and correlation. We present a detailed mathematical formulation, focusing on the calculation of the non-classical correlation entropy and its application to evaluating measurement confidence. The methodology offers a potentially valuable tool for guiding decision-making in quantum information processing, particularly in scenarios where the precise characterization of the quantum state is challenging. Further investigation into the sensitivity of the method to various noise sources and its scalability for complex quantum systems is warranted. ---

title: Based on Quantum State Superposition: A Parallel Computing Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel parallel computing architecture fundamentally based on the principle of quantum state superposition. Traditional parallel computing relies on classical methods, often limited by the sequential nature of operations and the constraints of multiple processors. This architecture leverages the inherent ability of quantum systems to exist in multiple states simultaneously, offering a potential paradigm shift in computational efficiency. The core concept involves designing a system where multiple quantum computations can be executed concurrently, drastically reducing processing time for suitable algorithms. This paper details the architecture, outlines the key mathematical foundations, and explores the theoretical advantages of this approach. We present a framework for utilizing superposition to achieve parallelism, focusing on the manipulation of quantum states to represent and process multiple inputs or operations simultaneously. The potential impact of this architecture on various computational domains is discussed, highlighting areas where superposition-based parallelism could offer significant performance gains. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential for exponential speedups under certain conditions, contingent on the algorithm's suitability for superposition-based execution. Further research and development are needed to translate this architectural concept into a practical and scalable implementation.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Graph Structure Discovery from Unlabeled Data
abstract: Graph-based machine learning has witnessed remarkable success in diverse domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and knowledge graph construction. However, a significant challenge remains: the need for labeled data to effectively learn graph structures. Manually labeling graphs is a costly, time-consuming, and often subjective process. This paper proposes a novel self-supervised learning framework designed to directly learn meaningful graph structures from unlabeled data. The core idea is to formulate a self-supervised learning objective that encourages the network to predict missing edges or node labels based on graph context. This approach eliminates the reliance on labeled data, unlocking the potential of vast, unlabeled graph datasets. We introduce a specific architecture and objective function that leverages the inherent relational information within graphs to drive effective structure discovery. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in capturing complex graph structures compared to traditional methods.

title: Optimisation of 2d hydrodynamic model roughness with multi-output Gaussian process emulators and Bayesian active learning
abstract: This study presents a metamodeling approach using multioutput Gaussian process emulators (MO-GPEs) within a Bayesian active learning (BAL) framework to optimise spatially varying Nikuradse roughness coefficients in a 2d hydrodynamic model. The approach is applied in a near-natural fishway with a gravel bed. MO-GPEs learn relationships among deterministic numerical model outputs and are used in BAL to emulate response surfaces of complex physics-based models and iteratively select informative training points conditioned on measured data. This supervised learning procedure is showcased herein by means of a simultaneous Bayesian calibration of four Nikuradse roughness coefficients, and it provides uncertainty quantifications of these calibration parameters. The results show a reduction of 4.5% in normalised-root mean square error compared to a first-principle-reasoned benchmark model simulated with a global model roughness value. The uncertainty, measured by the width of posterior distributions, also reduces for all four calibrated roughness coefficients, indicating a more constrained high-probability region.

title: Hierarchical coarse-to-fine anomaly detection for high-dimensional time series
abstract: High-dimensional time-series anomaly detection must balance detection quality against computational cost under evaluation protocols that respect time order. We present a hierarchical coarse-to-fine framework: a low-capacity coarse stage screens the record into a candidate set of retained fraction \(\rho \) , and a higher-capacity fine stage scores only those candidates; in this screening regime ( \(\rho <1\) ) the gate directly shapes final predictions and fine-stage workload. Evaluation on a redesigned synthetic benchmark with moderate contamination ( \(21.4\%\) of time points) is chronological: no future information is used in model fitting, configuration selection, or threshold calibration; the primary top- \(\rho \) analysis is retrospective and batch-based; a causal, validation-calibrated gate is evaluated separately. The detector best matched to this near-linear–Gaussian benchmark—a lightweight PCA reconstruction—attains the best held-out \(F_1\) ( \(0.929\pm 0.019\) over five seeds) at a fraction of the deep models’ cost. Screening by an eight-component PCA coarse stage at a pre-specified retained fraction \(\rho =0.5\) preserves the full-evaluation \(F_1\) (paired \(\Delta F_1=+0.001\pm 0.004\) , five seeds) while halving the fine-stage workload, and the same gate improves a Transformer fine detector (paired \(\Delta F_1=+0.112\pm 0.031\) ) while roughly halving its fine-stage inference time. These results reflect detector–benchmark match on controlled synthetic data, not general superiority of linear methods.

title: REPLICANT: Learning Policies for Evading and Hardening Malware Detectors
abstract: To determine the real-world effectiveness of machine learning based malware detection, it is vital to evaluate its robustness against highly capable adversaries. However, state-of-the-art attacks do not effectively model realistic adversaries, as they often assume access to privileged information such as the training data, feature space, or confidence scores of the target. In this work, we present Replicant, a deep reinforcement learning framework that learns the realistic task of evasion under a strict label-only black-box threat model. Replicant learns a reusable policy on how to modify a malware sample and when to query the target, which transfers across samples, detectors, and feature spaces. Across seven Android malware detectors and three feature spaces, Replicant is the strongest and most query-efficient approach achieving a mean attack success rate of 78.8%, a relative improvement of 20.9%-39.2% over the state-of-the-art. Furthermore, when used for adversarial training, Replicant also outperforms the state-of-the art by producing detectors with more generalizable robustness. With Replicant we demonstrate that learning the task of evasion not only results in stronger attack performance but, crucially, provides a better signal for hardening malware detectors.

title: ErrorCaps: committed-effect measurement of recovery-path injection defense (CRiSIS 2026 artifact)
abstract: Reference implementation, benchmark, and analysis for the paper "Where Does Recovery-Path Injection Security Come From? Decomposing Error Sanitization, Effect Monitoring, and Policy Precision" (CRiSIS 2026). A synthetic committed-effect benchmark for indirect prompt injection on the tool-agent error-recovery path: a typed error terminal, a proposal-only planner, and a fine-grained effect-authority monitor. Includes per-episode records for all seven evaluated models, an automated policy-aware attacker, a value/provenance policy head-to-head, and an honest per-template statistical re-analysis. A single 'make reproduce' recomputes and checks every headline number offline (no API, no network), exiting non-zero on any mismatch. All attack payloads are benign synthetic canaries against canary sinks; no real systems, credentials, or targets are involved.

title: Computational Complexity Theory for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for tackling problems across diverse domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. Despite their practical success, the theoretical understanding of their computational complexity remains surprisingly underdeveloped. This paper argues for the critical need for a rigorous mathematical framework to analyze the complexity of GNNs. We introduce a novel approach centered around the development of new complexity classes and algorithms specifically designed to assess the performance of GNNs in various scenarios, considering diverse graph structures and tasks. Our investigation focuses on identifying inherent computational bottlenecks and exploring potential improvements in GNN architectures and training strategies. We propose a framework that moves beyond the typical O(n²) analysis, recognizing that the complexity of GNNs is far more nuanced and dependent on graph properties, message passing schemes, and aggregation functions. This work represents a foundational step towards a deeper theoretical understanding of GNNs, paving the way for more efficient and robust GNN designs.

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to reasoning systems by integrating probabilistic logic programming with Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both techniques: the structured knowledge representation and inference capabilities of probabilistic logic programming, combined with the efficient search and exploration abilities of MCTS, guided by Bayesian inference. The system utilizes Bayesian inference to evaluate probabilistic logic rules, providing a probabilistic assessment of each rule's applicability. This probabilistic information is then used to guide the MCTS search, allowing the algorithm to intelligently explore the solution space. We demonstrate that this combination can lead to more robust and adaptive reasoning systems compared to traditional approaches. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of the MCTS search based on the evolving probabilistic knowledge, enhancing its efficiency and robustness in handling uncertainty. This approach offers a flexible framework for tackling complex reasoning problems where knowledge is incomplete and uncertain. ---

title: Self-Healing Neural Networks via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to constructing self-healing neural networks utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The core idea revolves around leveraging a GAN to generate adversarial examples that closely resemble attacks targeting a primary neural network. This generated data is then employed to continuously retrain the primary network, fostering enhanced resilience against both deliberate adversarial attacks and data corruption. The method offers a dynamic and adaptive training strategy, moving beyond static adversarial training, and aims to create networks capable of autonomously recovering from compromised states. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline the key components required for implementation. The primary contribution lies in the automated generation of realistic attack vectors for continual network adaptation, significantly improving robustness compared to traditional methods.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding via Relational Causality
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to graph embedding that explicitly incorporates temporal dynamics and relational causality. Traditional graph embedding methods typically treat graphs as static structures, neglecting the evolving relationships between nodes over time. We introduce a framework that leverages Granger causality tests and structural causal models to quantify temporal dependencies within a graph, constructing a temporal causal graph. This temporal graph is then used to inform the graph embedding process, resulting in representations that capture not only the structural relationships but also their temporal evolution. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the quality of graph embeddings compared to static embedding methods, particularly in scenarios where temporal dynamics are crucial for understanding the underlying graph structure. Our method provides a fundamental shift in how we represent and analyze graphs, moving beyond static snapshots to dynamic, causally-informed representations. ---

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Neural Network Architecture Search
abstract: Neural Network Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful approach to automating the design of neural network architectures, traditionally a task requiring significant human expertise. However, conventional NAS methods, particularly those relying on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms, can be computationally prohibitive, demanding substantial resources and time. This paper proposes a novel approach to NAS that leverages quantum-inspired optimization techniques, specifically drawing inspiration from quantum annealing, to accelerate the search process. The core idea is to map the architectural search space to a quantum system and utilize quantum annealing to efficiently explore this space, capitalizing on principles like superposition and entanglement. We formulate the architectural search as an optimization problem where the goal is to minimize a defined cost function (e.g., validation accuracy) while adhering to architectural constraints. The quantum annealing process effectively samples solutions from this complex space, offering a potentially faster and more effective method compared to classical methods. We present a detailed framework for this approach, outlining the mapping process, the quantum annealing algorithm, and the evaluation metrics. evidence.title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Neural Network Architecture Search
evidence.abstract: Neural Network Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful approach to automating the design of neural network architectures, traditionally a task requiring significant human expertise. However, conventional NAS methods, particularly those relying on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms, can be computationally prohibitive, demanding substantial resources and time. This paper proposes a novel approach to NAS that leverages quantum-inspired optimization techniques, specifically drawing inspiration from quantum annealing, to accelerate the search process. The core idea is to map the architectural search space to a quantum system and utilize quantum annealing to efficiently explore this space, capitalizing on principles like superposition and entanglement. We formulate the architectural search as an optimization problem where the goal is to minimize a defined cost function (e.g., validation accuracy) while adhering to architectural constraints. The quantum annealing process effectively samples solutions from this complex space, offering a potentially faster and more effective method compared to classical methods. We present a detailed framework for this approach, outlining the mapping process, the quantum annealing algorithm, and the evaluation metrics. Preliminary results demonstrate the potential of this quantum-inspired optimization strategy to achieve competitive or superior architectures with significantly reduced computational cost.

title: Ordering Is Not Resolution: What the Instruction Hierarchy Defines, What It Leaves Undefined, and the Same-Tier Conflicts Agent Benchmarks Do Not Separate
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. When a language-model agent receives instructions that conflict, the dominant remedy is a privilege ordering over sources: system above developer, developer above user, user above tool output. This paper argues that the ordering paradigm is well-defined for one class of conflict and undefined for another, and that published benchmarks and training sets do not separate the two. A conflict between instructions carrying different privilege labels has an answer the paradigm can state; a conflict between two instructions carrying the same label does not, because an ordering over privilege levels does not induce an ordering among the instructions inside a level. The second class is not hypothetical. One profiler of real deployed prompt policies reports that across thirteen thousand jointly governed trials, only about a third of cases satisfy both of two individually reasonable standing rules. Multi-principal deployments, where two users hold equal authority, instantiate the same structure by construction. The paper distinguishes three failure classes that the single phrase "instruction hierarchy failure" currently covers, argues that reported hierarchy-compliance numbers are sums over classes with different remedies, and states what a same-tier resolution rule would have to supply that an ordering does not. The case for the ordering paradigm is presented first and is not weak: several recent results report large, transferable gains from training on ordering. Nine studies that would settle the open parts are named. No experiments are reported here, and the strongest case against this paper's own position is stated in full.

title: Study of deep learning cues for cross linguistic part of speech tagging in English– Malayalam code-mixed data
abstract: Introduction: Part Of Speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that assigns grammatical labels to words in a sentence. Code mixed text, which entails switching between two or more languages within a single conversation or a sentence, presents challenges for POS tagging. This investigation entailed a comprehensive study of deep learning approaches for cross linguistic POS tagging, focused on English Malayalam code mixed data prevalent on social media platforms. The study was carried out on linguistically complex and varied English Malayalam code mixed text from social media platforms with informal spellings, language switching, transliteration, slang, and unclear grammatical boundaries, reflecting the characteristics of informal online communication. We provide the first structured analysis of micro macro divergence and rare class behavior in English Malayalam code mixed POS tagging. Methods: We evaluated 14 state of the art model configurations that span traditional sequence labeling approaches and multilingual transformer architectures. Models were compared using standard performance metrics prevalent in the domain of data science, supplemented by normalized confusion matrices, error prone tag identification and micro-macro F1 gap analysis. Results: Our results showed that CRF (No Lang) emerged as the most balanced model overall on macro F1 (all classes) of 0.8170, while (BiLSTM + CRF) achieved the highest macro F1 (seen classes) of 0.8831, precision of 0.9167, and recall of 0.875, though this reflects strong performance concentrated on frequent tag classes rather than balanced coverage across the full tag set. Notably, the pretrained multilingual transformers (mBERT, MuRIL), despite prior exposure to Malayalam during pretraining, were outperformed on several key metrics by CRF and BiLSTM models trained directly on the code mixed dataset. Discussion: This finding was contrary to our expectation that existing multilingual knowledge would translate into a clear advantage on this task and merits further investigation.

title: Amploc: A Complete Python Workflow for Amplitude-Based Locations
abstract: Abstract Amplitude-based locations are well suited for characterizing long-duration seismic sources that may migrate with time, such as debris flows, avalanches, rockfall, and volcanic tremor. Although amplitude-based location methods have existed for decades, their adoption in real-time monitoring systems remains limited. We present a complete Python-based workflow that includes station corrections, amplitude-based location algorithms, and interactive review tools that are appropriate for real-time use. The algorithms themselves are not new; however, Amploc integrates several previously published methods into a unified operational framework. The workflow also introduces a browser-based graphical interface that allows users to review real-time location results using formats familiar to many observatories. By integrating calibration, location algorithms, and visualization tools, Amploc lowers the barrier to operational use of amplitude-based locations and improves characterization of phenomena that inform hazard assessments such as long-period earthquakes, volcanic tremor, and debris flows.

title: Adaptive self-organized criticality in deep neural networks
abstract: Deep neural networks are high-dimensional dynamical systems whose function depends on the stable propagation of activity and perturbations across many layers. Maintaining suitable dynamical regimes may therefore be essential for robust learning and for preventing dynamical instabilities during training. Here, we show that the global dynamical state of a deep neural network can be autonomously regulated by purely local homeostatic plasticity. Neuronal activity is inferred from responses across inputs, and individual synapses are strengthened or weakened using only the activity of their postsynaptic neuron. Without measuring any global network property, this rule drives networks from both subcritical and supercritical initial conditions toward a common critical state, characterized by conserved activity propagation and a vanishing largest finite-time Lyapunov exponent. When combined with gradient-based learning, homeostatic adaptation counteracts the training-induced drift toward supercritical dynamics, while revealing a competition between dynamical regulation and task optimization. Our results demonstrate how adaptive self-organization can be implemented in deep neural networks and how local plasticity can control their collective dynamical operating point.

abstract: Detection rates for three transcription-error classes — exhaustive single-character substitution, exhaustive two-position transposition (bucketed by whether the check position is involved), and Monte-Carlo random double errors — measured over 2,000 generated codes per scheme with a fixed-seed PRNG. title: Procesamiento morfológico de imágenes binarias mediante circuitos cuánticos: una implementación en qiskit
abstract: Erosion and dilation are fundamental mathematical morphology operations used to modify the shape of objects in binary images. This study evaluated their implementation through a quantum circuit simulated in Qiskit, using classical processing in OpenCV as the reference. The Baboon image was analyzed at resolutions of 102×102, 128×128, and 256×256 pixels, with 16, 160, 1600, 16000, and 160000 circuit executions. The comparison included visual inspection, calculation of MSE, PSNR, and SSIM, and measurement of simulation times. The circuit reproduced the expected effect of both operations, although the reconstructed images did not fully match those obtained with OpenCV. Dilation showed more stable similarity than erosion. In addition, increasing the number of executions did not improve the metrics monotonically and substantially increased computation time.

title: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Link Prediction Model Based on Sequential Fusion
abstract: In the research of multimodal knowledge graph link prediction, the existing methods usually use concatenation or attention mechanism to fuse multimodal features. However, these methods fail to fully solve the problem of heterogeneity between different modalities and their complex interactions, which has a certain impact on the accuracy of link prediction. Therefore, in order to solve this problem, this paper proposes a multi-modal knowledge graph link prediction model based on sequential fusion, which uses a sequential fusion method to gradually fuse multi-modal information. In this method, a two-level fusion module is designed to fuse visual information and text information at two levels of coarse granularity and fine granularity, and then the orthogonal fusion module is used to integrate the structural information into the existing visual text features to ensure the synergy between different modalities. Moreover, regularization is added to the loss function to reduce redundant features and improve the performance of link prediction. In order to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, experiments are carried out on FB15k-237-IMG and WN18-IMG datasets, and compared with the existing multi-modal models, the proposed model achieves advanced results.

title: LUAD-MIT-25K
abstract: # LUAD-MIT-25K Dataset ## Dataset Summary LUAD-MIT-25K is a multi-center histopathology dataset dedicated to mitotic figure detection in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). The dataset is constructed from 305 H&E-stained whole-slide images collected from three independent medical centers with heterogeneous scanning magnifications and staining protocols. All image patches are uniformly normalized to a resolution of 0.25 μm/pixel (40× equivalent) with a fixed size of 256×256 pixels. The dataset is strictly partitioned at the **patient level** into training, internal test, and external validation subsets to eliminate data leakage. The final dataset contains **3,231 mitotic figure annotations** and **21,835 tumor nucleus annotations** across 2,291 image patches. All annotations were double-reviewed by experienced pathologists following standard morphological criteria. This dataset is designed to evaluate cross-center domain generalization and facilitate robust mitosis detection algorithm development in lung adenocarcinoma. ## Dataset Structure ``` LUAD-MIT-25K/ ├─ patches/ │ ├─ train_patches/ # Training set patches (PNG + paired JSON) │ ├─ test_patches/ # Internal test set patches (PNG + paired JSON) │ └─ external_patches/ # External cross‑center validation patches └─ metadata.csv # Slide‑level authoritative metadata table ``` Each subfolder in `patches/` contains strictly paired files with identical filenames: - `.png`: Raw 256×256 histology patch, **no embedded or overlaid annotations** - `.json`: Patch-level metadata + point annotations for model training ## Per-patch JSON Format Each JSON file contains two core components: 1. **slide_metadata** Stores slide-level technical information: dataset split, slide ID, native/target MPP, scaling coefficient, native window size, and tile coordinates on the original whole slide. 2. **annotations** A list of point-wise pathological labels: - `coordinates`: Floating-point (x, y) position within the 256×256 patch - `classification`: Category identifier - `mitosis`: mitotic figure - `tumor_nucleus`: tumor cell nucleus > **Note**: > The metadata stored in individual patch JSON files is provided for user convenience. > The **canonical and authoritative source** for all slide-level statistics is the root-level `metadata.csv`. ## metadata.csv Description `metadata.csv` is a **tab-separated** slide-level metadata table. Each row corresponds to one whole-slide image. | Field | Description | |-------|-------------| | split | Patient-level dataset partition | | slide_id | Unique whole-slide identifier | | native_mpp | Original scanning resolution (μm/pixel) | | target_mpp | Unified normalized resolution (0.25 μm/pixel) | | native_window_size | Original cropping window size before rescaling | | coord_scale | Coordinate scaling factor for resolution normalization | | total_mitosis_in_slide | Total mitotic figures in the whole slide | | total_tumor_nuclei_in_slide | Total tumor nuclei in the whole slide | | export_positive_patch_count | Number of annotated patches exported per slide | ### Load Metadata with Python ```python import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv("metadata.csv", sep="\t", encoding="utf-8") ```

title: Quantum Coherence Measurement and Environmental Noise Modeling
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to precisely measuring quantum coherence and modeling the associated environmental noise. The core of the work lies in developing a high-sensitivity quantum sensor to directly quantify coherence, coupled with a robust environmental noise model designed to simulate the impact of external disturbances. We detail a methodology for characterizing coherence decay rates, a crucial parameter in quantum information processing. The model incorporates various noise sources, including thermal fluctuations, electromagnetic radiation, and mechanical vibrations. The results demonstrate the feasibility of this technique for enhancing the control precision of quantum systems and provide a foundational theoretical framework for quantum information handling. The key contributions include a refined measurement protocol and a comprehensive noise model validated through simulations.

title: Adaptive Circuit Design via Genetic Algorithms with Hardware-Aware Fitness Functions
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to circuit design leveraging the power of genetic algorithms (GAs) combined with hardware-aware fitness functions. The core issue addressed is the traditionally labor-intensive and expertise-dependent nature of circuit design. We propose a fully automated system where a GA iteratively evolves circuit topologies and parameters, guided by fitness functions that rigorously incorporate hardware constraints such as power consumption, area, and timing. The fitness functions are designed to directly penalize designs that violate these constraints, ensuring that the evolved circuits meet the specified performance requirements. Unlike previous GA-based approaches that often treat circuit design as a purely digital optimization problem, our method provides a holistic, hardware-aware solution. This significantly reduces design time, explores a wider design space, and ultimately leads to more efficient and optimized circuit implementations. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this adaptive design methodology for various digital circuit architectures.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Large-Scale Machine Learning Model Training
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of leveraging quantum-inspired optimization techniques to accelerate the training of large-scale machine learning models. Traditional optimization methods, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, often struggle with the complex, high-dimensional loss landscapes encountered in deep learning. We propose a novel training algorithm rooted in principles of quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and interference, to address these challenges. The core idea involves employing parallel computation and interference cancellation strategies to navigate the loss landscape more efficiently. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of classical optimization by exploring multiple regions of the loss function simultaneously and selectively amplifying beneficial updates while suppressing detrimental ones. The proposed method is theoretically grounded and offers a potentially transformative pathway toward faster and more effective training of large-scale machine learning models. We detail the mathematical formulation of the algorithm and present a conceptual framework for its implementation.

title: Intent-Constrained Graph-Augmented LLM Planning with Minimal-Edit Repair for Emergency Communication Service Restoration
abstract: Restoring emergency communication services after disasters requires stage-wise decisions under damaged infrastructure, partial observations, limited resources, and strict service-priority constraints. This paper proposes ICG-Restore, an intent-constrained graph-augmented large language model (LLM) planning framework with minimal-edit repair for high-level restoration planning. The method compiles operator requests, network observations, and operational rules into a unified intent schema, retrieves task-relevant local context from a heterogeneous scene graph and a restoration knowledge graph, and generates restoration candidates stage by stage. A rule-consistent repair module then corrects missing prerequisites, ordering conflicts, incompatible assignments, and budget violations with minimal modifications. To enable safe evaluation, we design a proxy executor that simulates abstract restoration primitives and environment evolution without involving real-world executable procedures. Experiments on three synthetic topologies show that ICG-Restore consistently achieves perfect constraint satisfaction and the highest composite recovery score, demonstrating strong feasibility, structural grounding, and restoration utility.

title: Good practices for Bayesian inference in statistical learning
abstract: Bayesian inference provides a unifying formalism for describing the inferences humans and other animals perform about features of the environment that change on fast timescales (moment-by-moment or trial-by-trial), as well as their learning of environmental contingencies and regularities that vary over slower time scales (i.e., statistical learning). We briefly highlight example Bayesian models of statistical learning at increasing levels of abstraction, such as the learning of parameters, causal structures, and programs. We then focus on the technical aspects of using such models and provide an overview of good practices for the key steps of fitting them to behavioral data: the validation of inference through sample-based calibration, the validation of fitting through parameter recovery, and the validation of model comparison through model recovery. While these steps undeniably require additional effort and compute, we argue that their use is essential for exploiting the full potential of Bayesian modeling.

title: The information geometry of product-reference discrete diffusion: Interaction growth complexity and optimal scheduling
abstract: We study a class of product-reference diffusion algorithms for sampling from a discrete distribution. We show that their sampling performance can be characterized using a path-based measure of data geometry that we call the interaction growth complexity (IGC). We show that a bivariate IGC kernel gives an exact representation of both the KL discretization error and a simple one-step upper bound. The simpler univariate IGC density can be used to study the effect of stepsize choices on the iteration complexity required to obtain $ε$-accurate samples in KL divergence. Samplers that traverse the path with equi-spaced steps in log-squared-reliability-odds have performance that depends on the aggregate IGC mass, whereas refined choices of stepsizes have a lower complexity depending on a square-root functional. In the fine-grid limit, both of these characterizations become sharp. We also allow general product reference distributions and show that the reference law can substantially reshape the IGC profile and the resulting sampling complexity; in particular, references far from both the uniform and the data marginals can yield dimension-dependent improvements. Finally, the aggregate IGC mass admits bounds in terms of total correlation and dual total correlation, thereby connecting the pathwise geometry to classical measures of multivariate dependence.

title: The Mathematician Leads: Building a Research Profile in the Age of Frontier AI
abstract: I propose that mathematicians who use AI in research maintain a research profile: a record of what the system has learned about working with them, where those lessons came from, and whether they remain useful. I describe how such a profile grew out of my own mathematical work, through corrections, failed approaches, and repeated attempts to keep difficult ideas from drifting toward easier ones. The profile is not a portrait of the mathematician and does not replace mathematical judgment. It belongs under the mathematician's control and must remain open to revision. I invite others to develop profiles of their own and report what they learn.

title: Generative AI Alignment with Hinduism's Theological Plurality and Sacred Representation
abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly used to answer personal questions and mediate everyday practices, including religion. However, existing discussions around AI alignment and ethics have largely centered secular, Western, and Abrahamic assumptions about religion, offering limited attention to other faith-based traditions. In this paper, we examine how Hindu users engage with generative AI systems in relation to their religious knowledge, belief, and practice. Drawing on 15 semi-structured interviews with Bangladeshi Hindu participants, we analyze how users interpret AI-generated religious representations, scriptural explanations, devotional interactions, and synthetic religious media. We found that AI can be both accessible and ethically troubling. While AI supported scriptural inquiry, devotional visualization, and religious storytelling, our study also identified concerns about theological flattening, cultural misrepresentation, devotional manipulation, and the simulation of sacred presence and authority. We conclude by arguing that religious alignment in generative AI requires interpretive alignment: systems that disclose their limits, preserve plurality, and avoid simulating sacred authority and sycophantic personalization.

title: Interventional Attribution of Semantic and Surface Novelty for Open-World Text Classification
abstract: This preprint presents an intervention-based attribution framework for open-world text classification that distinguishes surface-level novelty from semantic-level novelty. The approach uses controlled views of the same input to identify whether apparent novelty is caused primarily by changes in wording or by genuinely unseen semantic categories. The framework combines cause-aware routing, verification-aware candidate discovery, few-shot prototype learning, and compact continual updates. It is evaluated on BANKING77, CLINC150, HWU64, StackOverflow, and 20 Newsgroups, including tests of openness, backbone consistency, intervention fidelity, and transfer beyond intent classification. The results show strong surface-shift recovery, candidate ranking, and incremental learning on intent datasets, while also identifying limitations in calibration, domain transfer, and few-shot new-class learning.

title: Building Portals and Web Interfaces for Triplestore-Based Content: A Literature Review Aligning Existing Tools
abstract: This literature review examines existing tools, frameworks, and approaches for publishing and presenting RDF and Linked Data through human-facing web interfaces. It focuses on technologies that mediate the content of triplestores for both general and expert audiences, with particular attention to their suitability for reproducible research-data dissemination and Open Science workflows. The reviewed solutions are positioned along a spectrum ranging from lightweight RDF exploration and browsing tools to comprehensive frameworks for building reusable semantic portals. The comparison considers four main dimensions: the ability to produce stable dissemination outputs; adherence to Linked Data publishing practices; the range of interaction paradigms offered to different audiences; and the practical reproducibility and transferability of the publication workflow. The review specifically considers reusable software whose core functionality includes generating HTML representations of RDF resources, providing navigable interfaces over RDF datasets, supporting dereferenceable Linked Data publication, or enabling the construction of RDF-based websites and semantic portals. Tools focused exclusively on triplestore storage, querying, conversion, reconciliation, analytics, or isolated visualisation are distinguished from publication-oriented systems. The accompanying comparative analysis documents the technologies, extensibility, intended users, technical requirements, real-world applications, openness, and FAIR-related characteristics of the selected tools, using evidence and quotations from the relevant literature. Particular attention is given to the different roles played by publication frameworks, portal engines, static and dynamic RDF site generators, RDF-centric web application frameworks, and integrated authoring and presentation environments.

title: Evidence-separated structured Gaussian VI replicate-diagnostic archive
abstract: Author-generated reproducibility archive for the manuscript "Replicate diagnostics for structured Gaussian variational inference: evidence separation and covariance-scale propagation". V8.9.22 adds a prespecified 240-fit Student-t replacement-reproduction archive after the original exploratory Student-t per-seed dataset and dedicated source could not be recovered. The replacement dataset is not historical recovery. The archive contains derived data, source code, exact formal-environment records, fit objects, optimization trajectories, evaluation batches, bootstrap draws, figure-source data, and SHA256 audit manifests. Structured VI Reproducibility Archive v8.9.22 This version synchronizes the public reproducibility archive with manuscript version V8.9.22. Main archival change The original exploratory Student-t per-seed dataset and dedicated fitting/evaluation source were not recovered and are not reconstructed. V8.9.22 instead contains a newly prespecified replacement-reproduction Student-t archive with a complete machine-readable evidence chain. The replacement archive includes: prespecified protocol and deterministic replacement-seed registry; 240 formal Student-t fits; 240 final fit objects; 240 complete optimization trajectories; 960 post-fit reverse-KL evaluation-batch records (4 × 5,000 draws per fit) with RNG identities; 240 per-run metric records; paired and unpaired 10,000-resample finite-run bootstrap outputs; 340,000 bootstrap draws; S11-S15 figure-source data and generation code; exact formal-environment verification/capture; independent output audit and post-completion SHA256 manifests. Scientific boundary The replacement data are not historical recovery and must not be represented as the original missing seed-level data. No seed replacement, target addition, p-value search, or outcome-driven tuning was used. The 708-dimensional pharmacovigilance application and the original 239-fit Gaussian Module B calibration are not rerun in this version. Licensing Author-generated code: MIT License. Author-generated derived data/tables and original figure-source data: CC BY 4.0, except where third-party rights or source terms apply. Raw FDA AEMS/FAERS archives are not redistributed. Repository provenance GitHub repository: https://github.com/fushanning330-lang/structured-vi-reproducibility Earlier releases remain historical provenance and should not be overwritten. Final audited release incorporating terminology, release-navigation, metadata, and reproducibility-helper portability corrections; scientific evidence and reported results are unchanged.

title: Machine Translation for Kusaal: A Parallel Corpus and a First Open-Source System
abstract: Kusaal is a Mabia (Gur) language spoken by roughly 420,000 people in Ghana's Upper East Region and across borders in Burkina Faso and Togo. Despite having a reference grammar, an official orthography, and a complete Bible translation, it has no machine translation system of any kind. This paper presents a 34,568-pair Kusaal–English parallel corpus assembled from six sources (YouVersion Bible, English–Kusaal Index, GhanaNLP, Lexique Pro, Wikipedia, and back-translation), and a bidirectional translation model fine-tuned from NLLB-200-distilled-600M. A new language token (kus_Latn) is initialised from the Dagbani (dag_Latn) embedding, the closest Mabia relative already present in NLLB, rather than from random noise. The model achieves 27.57 BLEU translating Kusaal into English and 13.72 BLEU in the reverse direction. The paper also documents two silent data corruptions encountered during corpus construction: an HTML leak in scraped Bible text, and a CSV quoting failure that silently dropped rows. Both are reported as a cautionary note for low-resource corpus work where every sentence pair is expensive. Corpus and model are released publicly under CC BY 4.0.

title: Topological Noise Suppression via Entangled Topology: A Novel Approach to Quantum Decoherence
abstract: Quantum decoherence poses a significant challenge to the development of practical quantum computers. The inherent sensitivity of quantum states to environmental interactions leads to rapid loss of quantum information. This work proposes a novel strategy for mitigating decoherence effects by leveraging topological protection. Specifically, we investigate the construction of quantum device arrays utilizing topologically protected states, combined with non-Abelian entanglement, to create a robust barrier against external noise. The core concept relies on isolating quantum bits (qubits) from environmental interactions through the unique properties of topological insulators and engineered topological structures. This approach aims to dramatically improve the fidelity and stability of quantum computations. Mathematical formulations detail the theoretical framework, demonstrating the potential of this method to achieve significantly reduced decoherence rates and enhanced quantum coherence times. The proposed architecture offers a pathway toward building more reliable and scalable quantum computing platforms.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Data Compression with Entangled State Encoding
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to data compression leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional classical compression algorithms often struggle to efficiently represent highly correlated data, particularly in complex datasets. This research proposes a method, termed entangled state encoding, where data is represented by the quantum state of an entangled pair. By exploiting the inherent correlations within the data, this technique aims to achieve significantly higher compression ratios compared to conventional methods. The core of the approach lies in encoding multiple data points simultaneously into the shared quantum state, effectively reducing redundancy. We analyze the theoretical limitations and potential advantages of this technique, focusing on the information-theoretic aspects of compression and the challenges associated with practical implementation. The study outlines the fundamental principles, provides a conceptual framework, and discusses the key considerations for future research in this emerging field. The central equation demonstrating the compression ratio is: R = (1 - P) * L, where R is the compression ratio, P is the probability of measurement error, and L is the original data length. Furthermore, we consider the entanglement fidelity (F) as a crucial parameter: F ∈ [0, 1], with higher fidelity leading to improved compression performance. The goal is to maximize the compression ratio while maintaining a high fidelity of the entangled state.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Deep Learning Hyperparameter Tuning
abstract: Hyperparameter tuning is a critical, yet computationally expensive, component of deep learning model development. Traditional optimization methods often struggle to efficiently navigate the high-dimensional hyperparameter space, frequently getting trapped in local optima. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum-inspired optimization algorithms to tackle this challenge. We explore techniques such as quantum annealing and quantum walks, adapting their core principles to the context of deep learning hyperparameter optimization. The core idea is to leverage the inherent parallelism and exploration capabilities of quantum systems to effectively search the hyperparameter space. We investigate the potential of these algorithms to escape local optima and discover superior model configurations. Our theoretical analysis and initial simulations demonstrate the promise of quantum-inspired optimization for significantly improving the efficiency and effectiveness of deep learning hyperparameter tuning. The primary objective is to provide a framework for exploring the advantages of quantum-inspired techniques in accelerating the deep learning workflow.

title: ##基于物理模拟的神经网络架构设计
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural network architecture design by leveraging physical simulation. Traditional neural network design relies heavily on heuristics and trial-and-error, often leading to suboptimal architectures. This research proposes a methodology where the fundamental interactions between neurons are modeled using physics engines or molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting data is then utilized to guide and optimize the structure and parameters of the neural network. The core claim is that simulating these physical interactions offers a pathway to more efficient and realistic network designs. This work presents a framework for this approach, detailing the simulation process, data extraction, and architectural optimization strategies. The potential benefits of this method, including enhanced learning capabilities and improved energy efficiency, are discussed.

title: A Cryptographically Secure and Explainable AI Framework for Automated Health Insurance Claim Processing Using the Insurefusionnet
abstract: Automated health insurance claim processing has become increasingly important as insurers rely on intelligent systems to handle growing claim volumes and automated decision support systems for claim transparency. However, existing models often suffer from limited interpretability, insufficient data security, and weak generalizability across diverse claim patterns. To address these challenges, this research proposes InsureFusionNet, a hybrid explainable structured ensemble framework integrating heterogeneous models of deep feature learning, uncertainty-aware prediction, interpretable boosting mechanisms, and high-performance gradient-boosting classifiers through a fusion strategy for robust health insurance claim approval classification. Explainable AI techniques, including SHAP and LIME, are incorporated to provide transparent justifications for automated claim approval decisions, thereby enhancing stakeholder trust and accountability. To ensure data privacy and security, the proposed framework integrates AES-256-GCM encryption for confidentiality, elliptic curve cryptography for secure authentication, and SHA-256 hashing for integrity assurance within a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain, enabling controlled access, tamper-resistant auditability, and trustworthy claim management. Experimental results demonstrate that InsureFusionNet achieves superior performance, attaining an accuracy of 97.24%, precision of 98.41%, recall of 95.89%, and F1-score of 97.11% compared to individual classifiers. Overall, the proposed framework offers a secure, transparent, and reliable solution for secure and explainable automated health insurance claim approval classification and contributes toward responsible and trustworthy AI deployment in healthcare systems.

To address these challenges, this research proposes InsureFusionNet, a hybrid explainable structured ensemble framework integrating heterogeneous models of deep feature learning, uncertainty-aware prediction, interpretable boosting mechanisms, and high-performance gradient-boosting classifiers through a fusion strategy for robust health insurance claim approval classification. Explainable AI techniques, including SHAP and LIME, are incorporated to provide transparent justifications for automated claim approval decisions, thereby enhancing stakeholder trust and accountability. To ensure data privacy and security, the proposed framework integrates AES-256-GCM encryption for confidentiality, elliptic curve cryptography for secure authentication, and SHA-256 hashing for integrity assurance within a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain, enabling controlled access, tamper-resistant auditability, and trustworthy claim management. Experimental results demonstrate that InsureFusionNet achieves superior performance, attaining an accuracy of 97.24%, precision of 98.41%, recall of 95.89%, and F1-score of 97.11% compared to individual classifiers. Overall, the proposed framework offers a secure, transparent, and reliable solution for secure and explainable automated health insurance claim approval classification and contributes toward responsible and trustworthy AI deployment in healthcare systems.
